title: Tuned Fitness Landscapes for Benchmarking Model-Guided Protein Design.
authors: Thomas, Neil; Agarwala, Atish; Belanger, David; Song, Yun S; Colwell, Lucy J
abstract: Machine learning-guided directed evolution (MLDE) is an emerging paradigm of protein design where ML models trained on experimental data are used to guide exploration of a protein fitness landscape. Building an MLDE pipeline involves many design choices across the design-build-test-learn loop ranging from data collection strategies to modeling. The cost of collecting experimental data makes benchmarking every component of these pipelines prohibitively difficult, necessitating the development of synthetic landscapes. In this work, we develop a framework called SLIP ("Synthetic Landscape Inference for Proteins") for constructing synthetic landscapes with tunable difficulty based on Potts models. This framework can be extended to any protein family for which there is a sequence alignment. We show that our tuning framework provides landscapes sufficiently challenging to benchmark MLDE pipelines. SLIP is open-source and is available at https://github.com/google-research/slip.

title: Self-Assembling Peptide Hydrogels for Mucosal Drug Delivery: Synthesis, Triggering Strategies, and Therapeutic Applications.
authors: Zheng, Xin; Jin, Susu; Zhu, Shuyao; Lee, Tao; Jin, Zhaohui
abstract: Self-assembling peptide hydrogels (SAPHs) have emerged as promising platforms for mucosal drug delivery due to their excellent biocompatibility, programmable sequence design, and diverse triggering strategies. This review systematically discusses the molecular basis, synthesis techniques, and triggering strategies of SAPHs, highlighting how these elements collectively enable in situ gelation and on-demand drug release at mucosal sites. We also review applications across the oral, gastrointestinal, ocular, vaginal, middle ear, and respiratory mucosa, demonstrating the therapeutic potential of SAPHs in infection treatment, tissue repair, and immunomodulation. We further compare SAPHs with other mucosal delivery systems and summarize the clinical status of mucosal delivery products; although several products are in clinical use, no SAPH-based product has been approved for mucosal delivery, and the factors limiting clinical translation are discussed. Despite significant progress, several challenges remain, including balancing mechanical stability with degradation, ensuring batch-to-batch consistency, confirming long-term biosafety, and obtaining regulatory approval. With the integration of artificial intelligence-assisted design and modular programmable platforms, SAPHs hold considerable promise for precision mucosal drug delivery.

title: The Effect of S616L, a CPVT1-Associated Mutation, on the Stability and Structure of Human Cardiac RyR2.
authors: Bauer, Jacob A; Benko, Mario; Sutova, Lubica; Beck, Konrad; Nowak, Jakub; Bellova, Jana; Barath, Peter; Bauerova-Hlinkova, Vladena
abstract: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia type 1 (CPVT1) is a heritable genetic disease caused by mutations to hRyR2, the cardiac isoform of the human ryanodine receptor. One such mutation, S616L, is found in the alpha-helical part (NSol) of the hRyR2 N-terminal domain (NTD) close to a three-way junction between the NTD, junctional solenoid (JSol), and bridging solenoid (BSol) domains. In this study, we use molecular dynamics simulation to study the effect of S616L on the residues of this junction. We find that the mutation slightly weakens the interface between the N-terminal domain and the bridging solenoid by changing the preferred conformation of the residues at the interface, thereby promoting a slight opening between these domains. In addition, we determined the impact of this mutation on the biophysical and biochemical properties of a 655-residue fragment containing the entire hRyR2 N-terminal domain, finding that it slightly increases the thermal stability of the fragment.

title: AI-Assisted Molecular Structure Prediction from Tandem Mass Spectra: Reliability and Validation.
authors: Yu, Jun Sang; Jeong, Sung Hue; Kim, Yejin; Lee, Dong Keun; Yoo, Hye Hyun
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has broadened the interpretation of tandem mass spectra (MS/MS) beyond experimental library matching, enabling molecular fingerprint prediction, candidate ranking, and generation of previously unlisted structures. Yet these outputs do not all support the same claim about chemical identity. This review briefly summarizes database-restricted retrieval, database-free generation, and scaffold-guided hybrid methods, and then asks what additional evidence is needed to turn a plausible structure into a defensible annotation. We examine failure modes involving incomplete candidate spaces, erroneous precursor assignments, structurally related isomers, leakage between training and test data, and misinterpreted confidence scores. The review contributes two practical elements: a candidate-discrimination workflow, in which alternative structures are retained and targeted measurements such as multienergy fragmentation, retention behavior, ion mobility, and authentic standards are selected according to the unresolved structural question; and an evidence-to-claim checklist that links each question to the most informative measurement and to the strongest supportable identification confidence level. Both synthesize established analytical principles for small-molecule electrospray LC-HRMS/MS rather than constituting a validated scoring algorithm. By making the basis of each annotation transparent, they are intended to improve the practical value of AI-assisted MS/MS in metabolomics, pharmaceutical analysis, environmental screening, and forensic toxicology.

title: Molecular Dynamics Reveals Structural Consequences of Schizophrenia-Associated SLC6A1 Variants.
authors: Abashkin, Dmitrii A; Abdurazakov, Amal; Marilovtseva, Ekaterina V; Semina, Ekaterina V; Chaika, Yulia A; Golimbet, Vera E
abstract: The SLC6A1 gene encodes the GAT-1 transporter, which mediates the reuptake of GABA in the central nervous system (CNS). Missense variants in this gene are associated with the development of neuropsychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia. Although in vitro assays demonstrate a loss of transport activity, they do not elucidate how specific amino acid substitutions disrupt local interactions within the protein. To delineate the structural consequences of these mutations, we analyzed the inward-open apo-state of human GAT-1 (PDB: 7Y7V) using microsecond-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. This study compares the wild-type transporter with mutant forms, including the schizophrenia-associated variants R211C and A305T, alongside the A346S variant selected via deep learning-based pathogenicity predictors. The results demonstrate that these mutations do not globally destabilize the protein structure; rather, they induce specific rearrangements within local contact networks. The R211C substitution abolishes a hydrogen bond at the interface of extracellular loop 2 (EL2) and transmembrane helix 4 (TM4). A305T alters the TM1-TM6 interface adjacent to the sodium ion-binding site, and A346S strengthens TM1/TM6-EL4 interactions. The identified structural shifts suggest how pathogenic mutations remodel the GAT-1 interaction network and alter its conformational dynamics. These findings provide a foundation for subsequent molecular docking aimed at drug repurposing and for comprehensive MD modeling of the complete GAT-1 transport cycle.

title: Beyond the Black Box: Physics-Based and Conservation-Informed Evidence for ACVRL1 Variant Classification in Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia and Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension.
authors: Brusgaard, Klaus
abstract: Missense variants in ACVRL1 (ALK1) cause hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia type 2 (HHT2), heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), or both in the same patient, and many remain variants of uncertain significance. AlphaMissense classifies them accurately but does not show which evidence drives a call. I annotated 899 ACVRL1 missense variants with protein-stability estimates (FoldX, DynaMut2), a GREMLIN-style conservation score, and structural context. I then trained random-forest classifiers on 311 variants with labels traceable to ClinVar or a publication (296 pathogenic-like, 15 benign-like). A structural/conservation-only classifier (Model 1b) reached a cross-validated ROC-AUC of 0.954 (95% CI 0.916-0.984), and a model adding sequence-based predictors (Model 1) reached 0.979, versus 0.983 for AlphaMissense on the same variants. On variants first reported in 2025-2026, Model 1b scored 0.976, Model 1 0.992, and AlphaMissense 0.992; equivalence within +/-0.05 AUC was supported for Model 1 only. Benign variants were the main weakness: Model 1b correctly classified 10/15, against 14/15 for AlphaMissense. Conservation drove most calls, with predicted destabilization contributing to a minority. An interpretable, gene-specific classifier can approach AlphaMissense for ACVRL1 while showing the structural or evolutionary evidence behind each call. Its calls are hypotheses, not functional evidence, and can prioritize VUS for functional testing.

title: Structural Determinants Underlying the Interplay Between Fatty Acid Binding and S-Nitrosylation of Human Serum Albumin.
authors: Batalova, Anastasia A; Samodurova, Kamila V; Vovk, Mikhail A; Belinskaia, Daria A; Jenkins, Richard O; Goncharov, Nikolay V
abstract: Human serum albumin (HSA) is a multifunctional protein whose biological properties are determined not only by its amino acid sequence but also by a complex interplay of functional sites, post-translational modifications, and endogenous ligands. However, the structural mechanisms by which these regulatory factors influence the functional state of HSA remain insufficiently understood. The aim of this study was to investigate the structural basis of the interplay between HSA functional regions, using Cys34 S-nitrosylation and fatty acid (FA) binding as model regulatory processes. For this purpose, the structural features and conformational dynamics of FA-free and FA-loaded native and nitrosylated HSA, as well as their interactions with glutathione (GSH) and S-nitrosoglutathione (GSNO), were studied using molecular docking and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Changes in the overall structure of HSA after incubation with GSNO were assessed by (1)H NMR spectroscopy. MD analysis revealed that FA binding alters the conformational dynamics of HSA and affects the structural environment of Cys34 and other functionally significant regions. These FA-induced effects were further modulated by S-nitrosylation, which influenced the conformational landscape of albumin in a manner dependent on its fatty acid-bound state. The similarity of the one-dimensional (1)H NMR spectra of HSA before and after incubation with GSNO suggests the absence of pronounced changes in the overall protein structure upon interaction with the nitrosylating agent. The obtained data provide insights into how FA binding and S-nitrosylation shape the conformational properties of HSA through modulation of the structural environment of Cys34 and other functionally significant regions. The results highlight the importance of considering post-translational modifications and endogenous ligands as key determinants of HSA structure-function relationships.

title: Emerging Computational Advances in Simulating PCSK9 Variant Dynamics for Therapeutic Design Against Hypercholesterolemia.
authors: Opazo, Ma Cecilia; Gallegos, Andres; Munoz, Antar; Zapata, Roger; Rivera, Juan Carlos; Sepulveda, Romina V; Aguayo, Daniel
abstract: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is a premier model for precision medicine, having moved from genetic discovery to approved therapeutics within two decades. Yet despite the clinical success of monoclonal antibodies, small interfering RNA and the newly approved oral macrocyclic-peptide inhibitor class, targeting PCSK9 remains a demanding biophysical challenge. Clinical translation has concentrated almost entirely on the rigid, well-resolved subtilisin-like catalytic domain that interfaces with the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR). By contrast, the C-terminal cysteine- and histidine-rich domain (CHRD), which governs allosteric regulation, protein trafficking and post-translational modification, is highly disordered and largely elusive in experimental structures, leaving a critical regulatory network therapeutically unexploited. This review examines how advanced computational biology is bridging that structural gap, organizing the computational landscape of PCSK9 around the biophysical mechanisms of gain- and loss-of-function variants. We detail how explicit-solvent molecular dynamics, free-energy calculations and cryptic-pocket detection expose the functional plasticity and allosteric networks that static crystallography cannot capture, and we evaluate the convergence of these physics-based approaches with artificial intelligence, including deep-learning structure prediction and generative design of de novo nanobody and peptide binders. Therapeutic development and the structural literature currently point in diverging directions: drug discovery remains focused on the crowded LDLR-binding interface, whereas computational methods are beginning to identify candidate sites beyond it. We argue that the next advance in PCSK9 therapeutics will come from integrating generative artificial intelligence with rigorous enhanced sampling in a unified pipeline, deliberately shifting focus toward the disordered regulatory domains that have evaded classical screening.

title: Molecular Dynamics Simulations Reveal a Broadly Open Solution Ensemble for the DNA Holliday Junction: Mg(2+) Crossover Bridging and Weak Force-Field Sensitivity.
authors: Zhang, Yonghui; Zhou, Yujia
abstract: Holliday junctions, four-way DNA crossovers central to DNA origami and key intermediates of homologous recombination, must be accurately modeled for rational DNA-nanodevice design, yet their solution conformational ensemble remains incompletely characterized. We characterize this ensemble for the experimental junction d(TCGGTACCGA)(4) by all-atom molecular dynamics, comparing the AMBER force fields parmbsc1, OL21, and OL24 in OPC water with matched ionic conditions. In every force field, the junction explores a broad, nearly flat inter-arm-angle landscape, with <1 kcal/mol variation across inter-arm angles of 2-90 degrees : the open state is favored by 0.45-0.63 kcal/mol, the crystallographic-like inter-arm angle occurs in 2-5% of frames, and the crossover remains coaxially stacked whether open or compact. A Mg(2+) ion occupies the crossover pocket in 92-94% of frames, specifically bridging the A- and C-strand phosphates (Li-Merz CM Mg(2+) set). Stacking-isomer exchange between the A/C-continuous and crystallographic B/D isomers proceeds at ~0.5 ns(-1) in this minimal short-arm construct, independent of force field, with A/C-continuous favored ~2:1. parmbsc1 yields a more open junction than OL21 and OL24, which reproduce the crystallographic inter-arm angle of 39-43 degrees ; the sugar-pucker shift targeted in OL24 is also visible at the junction. These results establish a force-field-robust baseline for simulation-guided design of crossover-containing nanostructures.

title: Discovery of Novel HDAC8 Inhibitors Through Shape-Based Virtual Screening: Experimental Validation and Characterization of a Promising Quinoline-Based Hit Scaffold.
authors: Gargano, Adriana; Gonzalez-Bakker, Aday; Puerta, Adrian; Maggisano, Valentina; Bulotta, Stefania; Rocca, Roberta; Padron, Jose M; Alcaro, Stefano
abstract: Histone deacetylase 8 (HDAC8) is overexpressed in several solid tumors and, unlike other Class I HDACs, functions independently of large corepressor complexes, making it an attractive target for structure-based drug design. Here, we aimed to identify novel natural compounds capable of targeting the human HDAC8 catalytic site. A library of 307,814 natural products from ZINC15 was screened by shape-based virtual screening using five structurally diverse co-crystallized HDAC8 ligands as templates, followed by molecular docking and Molecular Mechanics-Generalized Born Surface Area (MM-GBSA) binding free energy calculations. Seven commercially available hits were selected for enzymatic validation, leading to the identification of 4-((7-methoxyquinolin-4-yl)amino)benzamide (ZINC000054202375, compound 2) as a promising HDAC8 inhibitor. In vitro antiproliferative assays across multiple human solid tumor cell lines demonstrated significant growth inhibition by compound 2, further supported by colony formation assays. Mechanistic studies using label-free live-cell imaging, Annexin V staining, DAPI (4',6-diamidino-2-phenylindole) nuclear morphology, and DCFDA (2',7'-dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate) assays revealed membrane blebbing, mitotic failure, increased reactive oxygen species, and nuclear fragmentation, consistent with apoptosis induction. Finally, 1 mus molecular dynamics simulations supported the formation of a persistent ligand-receptor interaction network within the HDAC8 catalytic pocket. Overall, compound 2 represents a promising non-hydroxamate hit scaffold with promising HDAC8 inhibitory activity, serving as a starting point for the development of novel HDAC-targeted anticancer agents.

title: Structure-based virtual screening with AlphaFold identifies CLIP1-LTK inhibitors.
authors: Qu, Wang-Lin; Zhang, Xu-Jun; Wang, Gao-Ang; Tian, Wei-Xin; Chen, Kang; Ye, Yuan-Yi; Chen, Shi-Cheng; Hu, Ru-Bi; Liu, Yi-Fei; Shen, Chao; Li, Dan; Kang, Yu; Tian, Sheng; Teng, Peng; Hou, Ting-Jun; Pan, Pei-Chen
abstract: Artificial intelligence-based protein structure prediction provides new opportunities for structure-based drug discovery, especially for targets lacking experimental structures. Determining whether AlphaFold2- and AlphaFold3-derived models can reliably support structure-based virtual screening remains a critical issue. In this study, we systematically evaluated the applicability of AlphaFold2- and AlphaFold3-derived models for structure-based virtual screening and assessed the performance of different VS pipeline configurations that integrate AlphaFold models with diverse docking and scoring combinations. Based on our benchmarking results, we established a hierarchical VS methodology and applied this approach to CLIP1-LTK, an oncogenic fusion protein lacking an experimentally resolved structure. Using this pipeline, a library of approximately three million compounds was virtually screened, leading to the identification of potential inhibitor candidates. Similarity-based analog searching identified QL07, which exhibited an IC(50) value of 524.27 nM. QL07 inhibited CLIP1-LTK downstream signaling pathways and induced apoptosis in transformed Ba/F3-CLIP1-LTK cells. Furthermore, QL07 suppressed the growth of CLIP1-LTK-positive tumors in xenograft models. These findings underscore the utility of AlphaFold models in overcoming structural limitations in drug discovery and demonstrate their feasibility in identifying promising small-molecule inhibitors against protein targets without experimentally-determined structures.

title: Handshake: Partner-specific protein-protein binding site prediction at scale using ProstT5 and cross-chain attention.
authors: Haspel, Nurit
abstract: Partner-specific protein-protein binding site prediction, identifying which residues of a protein form the interface when bound to a specific partner, remains a challenging task with significant implications for drug discovery and understanding of protein structure and function. Existing computational methods are limited by small training datasets, inconsistent redundancy filtering, and reliance on three-dimensional structural information at test time. Here we present a sequence-only, partner-specific protein-protein interface predictor called HandShake. It combines ProstT5, a protein language model pre-trained on structural data, with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), a cross-chain attention mechanism and a contact supervision head. Our method can detect both binding interfaces and pairwise contact matrices. We trained our model on very large datasets of non-redundant protein-protein pairs derived from the PPInterface dataset, the most comprehensive structural protein-protein database to date, and evaluated it on systematically filtered benchmarks at four redundancy thresholds (30%-90% sequence identity). We demonstrate that sequence redundancy inflates reported AUROC by up to 0.079 and MCC by up to 0.145 on identical models, representing a substantial methodological confound in the field. Even at 30% redundancy threshold, our results (AUROC = 0.811, MCC = 0.367, F1 = 0.45) exceed the best published sequence-only result on this convention. Our method also achieves comparable performance to existing partner-specific methods that use explicit structural information. The comprehensive training and evaluation dataset, in addition to the systematic redundancy inflation, can help gain insight into protein-protein interactions and the abilities and limitations of current detection methods.

title: Addressing Eroom's Law: The Shift Toward Clinically Driven Artificial Intelligence in Drug Discovery.
authors: He, Jin-Zang; Huo, Zi-Xiang; Wang, Chen-Yu; Ye, Yan-Hong; Shi, Zheng-Jie; Sun, Jia-Lu; Meng, Ze-Yu; Wang, Na-Na; Ming, Han-Yue; Xu, Sen; Meng, Jian-Li; Wang, Shou-Ni
abstract: BACKGROUND: Pharmaceutical Research and Development (R&D) is characterized by high costs, lengthy timelines, and frequent clinical failure. Eroom's Law describes the historical decline in new drug approvals per unit of R&D expenditure. Artificial Intelligence-driven Drug Discovery (AIDD) offers new approaches to target identification, molecular design, and property prediction, but improved computational performance alone does not establish clinical benefit. OBJECTIVE: This narrative review examines how AIDD can facilitate transitioning from target identification to molecular design and clinical evaluation. METHODS: It discusses graph neural networks, structure prediction, and generative models alongside pharmacological and clinical evidence. Four dimensions structure the discussion: target structure and dynamics; subcellular localization and target accessibility; pharmacokinetics and binding kinetics; and clinical factors. They provide a qualitative framework for identifying evidence gaps, not a mathematical model or predictive tool for drug efficacy. A complementary target-molecule-clinical framework illustrates how experimental and clinical evidence can inform earlier stages of drug development. RESULTS: Clinical examples, including rentosertib and GTAEXS617, emphasize distinguishing design objectives, preclinical findings, and clinical observations. Rentosertib's phase IIa trial provides an early clinical signal, although its limited sample size and duration preclude conclusions regarding sustained benefit. Training-data bias, data leakage, limited interpretability, synthetic accessibility, and uncertain generalizability beyond the training domain remain important concerns. This review acknowledges selective coverage of the literature and study-design heterogeneity. CONCLUSION: Assessing whether AIDD can improve overall drug-development efficiency requires comparative evidence on development time, cost, safety, and clinical success. Experimental validation and longitudinal clinical follow-up remain essential for evaluating these outcomes.

title: Leveraging amino acid embeddings for accurate translation efficiency prediction.
authors: Terai, Goro; Asai, Kiyoshi
abstract: MOTIVATION: Accurate prediction of translation efficiency from mRNA sequences is an important step toward mRNA sequence design. In recent years, the widespread adoption of high-resolution ribosome profiling techniques, such as Ribo-seq, has led to rapid accumulation of large-scale datasets that capture the relationship between mRNA sequences and translation efficiency. This progress has facilitated the development of machine-learning-based models for translation efficiency prediction. However, most existing approaches rely primarily on mRNA-derived features, such as codon usage frequency and 5' untranslated regions (5'UTRs), and do not directly utilize the amino-acid-level information. RESULTS: In this study, we show that incorporating distributed representations (embeddings) of amino acid sequences translated from mRNA as model features can improve translation efficiency prediction. By combining fixed amino acid embeddings derived from a pretrained protein language model with mRNA-derived features, the proposed model integrates complementary protein-level and nucleotide-level information for more accurate prediction of translation efficiency. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Codes are available at GitHub (https://github.com/gterai/AA_emb) and Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23968476).

title: A Synthetic Benchmark for Topology-Aware Modeling of Multispecific Antibody Function.
authors: Southern, Joshua; Lu, Changpeng; Nerli, Santrupti; Stanton, Samuel D; Watkins, Andrew M; Seeger, Franziska; Dreyer, Frederic A
journal: Journal of computational biology : a journal of computational molecular cell biology
abstract: Multispecific antibodies (msAbs) offer transformative therapeutic potential by engaging multiple epitopes simultaneously, yet their efficacy is an emergent property governed by complex molecular architectures. Rational design is often bottlenecked by the inability to predict how subtle changes in domain topology influence functional outcomes, a challenge exacerbated by the scarcity of comprehensive experimental data. Here, we introduce Synapse, a biologically inspired synthetic benchmark for topology-aware modeling of msAbs. First, we present a generative method that combines nonlinear per-domain sequence-to-score landscapes with connectivity-dependent synthetic readouts. Second, we propose a graph neural network architecture that explicitly encodes these topological constraints, distinguishing between format configurations that appear identical to the evaluated connectivity-agnostic multilayer perceptron. We demonstrate that this model learns topology-dependent structure-function relationships on synthetic landscapes and evaluate a transfer learning workflow as infrastructure for adaptation to biological datasets. We showcase our framework with a trispecific T cell engager-inspired synthetic topology-dependent optimization task and a constrained ranking of common light chain candidates against a composite objective. This work provides a controlled benchmarking environment for developing and evaluating topology-aware computational tools for msAb modeling. All experiments use synthetic data; no biological validation is performed.

title: Mutational binding assessment for TCR engineering on experimental and AlphaFold 3 scaffolds.
authors: Guo, Zhongliang; Oyama, Kei; Yamaguchi, Rui
abstract: Machine learning-based binding affinity prediction can support T-cell receptor (TCR) engineering, but its reliability remains uncertain when experimental structures of TCRs bound to peptide-major histocompatibility complexes (pMHCs) are unavailable and predicted structures must be used instead. Here, we examined how AlphaFold 3 (AF3) scaffold choice and conformational sampling affect DeltaDeltaG -based prioritization of TCR-pMHC complementarity-determining region (CDR) mutations. Bound-unbound structural comparisons showed that pMHC binding is associated mainly with local CDR remodeling, especially in CDR3 loops, whereas TCR framework regions remain comparatively stable. AF3 generally recovered bound-like TCR conformations, but downstream DeltaDeltaG prediction performance depended strongly on both scaffold source and model architecture. These scaffold-dependent differences indicate that experimental structures remain the most reliable input when available, although such structures are rarely accessible in prospective TCR design settings. Among AF3-based inputs, Prompt-DDG and RDE-PPI were relatively robust to wild-type predicted scaffolds, whereas BA-DDG and H3-DDG benefited more from mutant-specific AF3 scaffolds evaluated by reverse-mutation scoring. Across four templates, AF3-mutant scaffolds gave the highest mean top-10 recovery among the AF3-based inputs for all four predictors. These results support using experimental structures when available and suggest using AF3-mutant scaffolds for recovering top-ranked CDR candidates when only predicted structures are available.

title: Transforming macromolecular structures into simulations of self-assembly with ioNERDSS.
authors: Ying, Yue Moon; Sang, Mankun; Au, Gabriel; Chhibber, Smriti; Du, Yufeng; Fischer, Jonathan A; Foley, Samuel L; Guo, Sikao; Herzog-Pohl, Ian; Liu, Zixiu; Roscom, Hannah; Sohail, Hassan; Takeshita, Sho S; Johnson, Margaret E
abstract: Macromolecular self-assembly is a fundamental process in living and engineered systems, producing molecular machines like the ribosome or highly symmetric viral capsids. Thanks to sources like the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and AlphaFold3, the final target complexes are often known, but these static structures do not provide information on the self-assembly process directly. Computational models provide critical tools to study these essential pathways of self-assembly, but substantial coarse graining of assembly subunits is necessary to achieve computational tractability of these relatively slow processes while retaining multi-valency. While local interactions overcome the often-prohibitive enumeration of all possible assembly intermediates, they must ensure global structural constraints are met. We here demonstrate ioNERDSS, a user-friendly Python package that transforms 3D atomic protein structures into coarse-grained (CG) models for immediate simulation with the stochastic reaction-diffusion NERDSS software, converting static structures into time-resolved assembly trajectories. With ioNERDSS, each protein chain is defined by a rigid subunit with discrete interfaces and explicit orientational constraints that enforce a structured assembly. Repeated subunits (such as in viral capsids) are regularized to preserve the target topology across distinct stochastic assembly pathways, supporting assembly of structures with thousands of subunits. We initialize pairwise binding affinities using ML prediction tools, and our default CG models are all constrained by thermodynamic reversibility to reach an equilibrium steady-state. The binding rates and subunit abundances necessary to perform simulations are initialized at default values but represent key variables that users should tune to test hypotheses on assembly pathways or to optimize models to experimental datasets. Benchmarking on over 50,000 PDB structures shows the majority of CG models will stochastically assemble into target structures. The ioNERDSS Python library links with open-source tools to facilitate fast and user-friendly structure validation and analysis of thermodynamic, kinetic, and nonequilibrium drivers of macromolecular self-assembly.

title: Structure-based discovery of inhibitors of Mac1 domain of nonstructural protein-3 of SARS-CoV-2 by machine learning-augmented screening of chemical space.
authors: Ban, Fuqiang; Ravichandran, Rahul; Correy, Galen J; Herasymenko, Oleksandra; Silva, Madhushika; Ackloo, Suzanne; Bolotokova, Albina; Chau, Irene; Gibson, Elisa; Harding, Rachel; Hutchinson, Ashley; Loppnau, Peter; Fraser, James S; Schapira, Matthieu; Cherkasov, Artem; Gentile, Francesco
abstract: Significant efforts have been recently dedicated to the discovery of small molecule inhibitors against the Macrodomain 1 (Mac1) of nonstructural protein 3 (NSP3) as potential antivirals for SARS-CoV-2. Thus, Mac1 has also been selected as the target for the Critical Assessment of Hit-finding Experiments (CACHE) challenge #3. As contestants in that challenge, we developed a computational strategy that ranked on the top among all 23 participants in the competition and resulted in the discovery of a novel chemical series of non-charged Mac1 inhibitors. Those have been identified through the combination of machine learning-accelerated virtual screening of Enamine REAL Diversity Subset of approximately 25 million compounds and consequent hit expansion into the entire Enamine REAL Space library. In particular, the initially identified hit compound CACHE3-HI_1706_56 (K(D) = 20 microM) was explored by probing 17 close analogues from a library of 44 billion molecules from the Enamine REAL. Most of those analogues effectively displaced the Mac1-binding ADP-ribose peptide, and 12 were confirmed to engage with Mac1 by Surface Plasmon Resonance experiments, revealing a new chemical series of compounds for hit-to-lead optimization. The structure of the CACHE3-HI_1706_56-Mac1 complex was further determined at high resolution with crystallography, confirming initial computational predictions. Our results illustrate the effectiveness of ML-accelerated docking to rapidly identify novel chemical series and provide a strong foundation for the development of SARS-CoV-2 NSP3 Mac1 inhibitors. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-65034-1.

title: Functional characterization and pharmacochaperone rescue of a novel SLC6A1 variant associated with developmental epileptic encephalopathies.
authors: Song, Ziang Debbie; DeLeeuw, Melissa B; Mandelenaki, Despoina; Shen, Wangzhen; Eda, Ria S; Wang, Juexin; Kang, Jing-Qiong
abstract: Mutations in SLC6A1, encoding the gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) transporter 1 (GAT-1), are associated with a spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders, including epilepsy syndromes, intellectual disability (ID), and autism. An important question is whether the impact of these mutations can be predicted at scale using artificial intelligence (AI), and how such predictions correlate with experimental findings. In this study, AI was explored as a predictive tool, not as a replacement for data collected experimentally. We reported clinical presentations including seizures and EEG features, autism related phenotypes and motor skills in a novel variant c.1069G > A (p.Ala357Thr, A357T) in two siblings. We used both AI tools and experimental approaches to characterize this novel mutation in the SLC6A1 gene and compared it with another variant in the same amino acid, c.1070 C > T (p.Ala357Val, A357V). Both AI and experimental approaches indicate that the GAT-1(A357T) and (A357V) mutations destabilize the global protein conformation and have increased localization inside the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Additionally, the presence of the mutant GAT-1 made the wildtype GAT-1 less mature. Radioactive (3)H-labeled GABA uptake assay indicated the mutation drastically reduced the function of the GAT-1(A357T) compared with the wildtype across cell types and pharmacochaperones such as 4-phenylbutyrate rescued the trafficking and function of the mutant GAT-1. Common and differential clinical phenotypes were identified in the siblings carrying the same variant. Mutant GAT-1 caused increased ER retention and impaired the trafficking of wild type GAT-1. PBA treatment rescued the mutant GAT-1 protein expression and GABA uptake function. AI-assisted in silico protein structural modeling and experimental approaches consistently suggest that the A357T and A357V variants destabilize global GAT-1 protein conformation. AI-assisted protein stability predictions provide supportive structural insight but cannot replace experimental assessment of GAT-1 expression and function. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-72601-z.

title: Distal amino-acid substitutions contribute to HIV protease inhibitor resistance as directly as proximal amino-acid substitutions.
authors: Das, Debananda; Hayashi, Hironori; Takamatsu, Yuki; Aoki, Manabu; Bulut, Haydar; Yedidi, Ravikiran S; Murayama, Kazutaka; Hasegawa, Kazuya; Ghosh, Arun K; Mitsuya, Hiroaki
abstract: There are two categories of drug-resistance-associated amino-acid substitutions responsible for causing drug resistance in HIV-1 protease: (i) major and (ii) minor substitutions. In general, major substitutions mostly arise early during treatment, reduce susceptibility to the drug and are mostly proximal to the protease active site. Minor substitutions mostly arise later, may provide incremental resistance and/or improve viral fitness and are often distal from the active site. However, no precise definitions of such two categories exist. Herein, using X-ray crystallography and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations we examined the structural basis of antiviral resistance of HIV(DRV) (R) (p51), an HIV-1 variant that has three proximal (V32I, V82I, I84V) and eleven distal substitutions (L10I/I15V/K20R/L24I/L33F/M36I/ M46L/ I54M/L63P/K70Q/L89M) in the protease region (PR(p51)), and has high resistance against a protease inhibitor darunavir (DRV), but not against another protease inhibitor GRL142. MD demonstrated that the proximal and distal substitutions work in concert to carry out structural changes that result in larger perturbations in inter-residue distances and active site cavity volume for DRV-PR(p51) over DRV-PR(wt) compared to GRL142-PR(p51) over GRL142-PR(wt). These results provided a rationale for the different resistance profiles of DRV and GRL142. The results also suggest reconsideration of the simplistic classification of substitutions as either major or minor. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-64620-7.

title: Markov state model for the forced unfolding of a small peptide.
authors: Oestereich, Marco; Gauss, Jurgen; Diezemann, Gregor
abstract: The mechanical unfolding of molecular complexes or biomolecules can routinely be studied using methods of single molecule force spectroscopy. In particular, the application of a force ramp with a constant pulling velocity in conjunction with stochastic modeling can be used to obtain valuable information regarding the relevant kinetics and the energy landscape. The computational counterpart of this type of experiment, using molecular dynamics simulations with atomistic resolution, allows us to gain insights into the molecular rearrangements underlying the unfolding process. However, due to the large difference in time scales, often coarse graining procedures are applied in the simulations. Most of the utilized techniques do not allow us to follow the atomistic details of the relevant conformational transitions due to the structural simplifications used to speed up the simulations. Here, we apply an earlier developed dynamic coarse graining technique based on Markov state modeling to a model peptidic system that does not unfold in a simple two-state manner. Using the donor-acceptor distances of the helical hydrogen bonds as collective variables and performing a dimension reduction allows us to construct a Markov model of the unfolding process that correctly represents the microscopic behavior of the system for not too fast pulling velocities. The chosen example shows that the method can be used to mimic the mechanical unfolding process of systems for which the end-to-end distance does not provide a sufficient order parameter and that do not unfold in a simple cooperative manner.

title: Terahertz-Driven Conformational Remodeling of Filamentous Actin: Insights into Intense Terahertz-Field-Mediated Biopolymer Responses.
authors: Liu, Chang; Zhang, Baolong; Shi, Chaojing; Liao, Guoqian; Wei, Yanyu; Ma, Jinglong; Ma, Ziyang; Zhu, Jiangrui; Li, Zhaoyu; Gao, Chutong; Zhang, Yaqun; Fu, Rao; Huang, Xiaorui; Liu, Ying; Qi, Feng; Ye, Fangfu; Guo, QianJin; Chen, Jianing; Wu, Xiaojun; Li, Ming; Fang, Weihai; Li, Yutong; Li, Yunliang
journal: The journal of physical chemistry letters
abstract: We demonstrate the precise, noninvasive control of filamentous actin (F-actin) conformations using high-intensity terahertz (THz) pulses via a dominantly nonthermal mechanism. By combining femtosecond time-resolved mid-infrared spectroscopy, Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, super-resolution confocal imaging, and a data-driven machine learning pipeline (CNN-UMAP-K-means), we show that 0.4 THz pulses selectively weaken intermolecular beta-sheet structures (1615 cm-1) while enhancing alpha-helical content (1650 cm-1) in F-actin, driving a dynamical shift toward monomer-like (G-actin) vibrational energy relaxation (VER) with up to 95% spectral similarity. In A549 cells, THz irradiation systematically reduces F-actin aggregation, as evidenced by fluorescence imaging. The spectral and dynamical changes induced by THz differ distinctly from thermal denaturation, with no characteristic peak shift observed under heating, supporting a dominantly nonthermal mechanism; our observations are consistent with coupling between intense terahertz fields and collective low-frequency intermonomer vibrational motions within F-actin filaments. The machine learning framework enables unbiased clustering and quantitative similarity analysis to identify optimal irradiation parameters (70 muJ, 10 min) that maximize selective F-actin remodeling without perturbing G-actin integrity. This work establishes intense THz as a powerful photonic tool for manipulating protein assemblies at molecular and cellular levels, advancing our fundamental understanding of THz-biopolymer interactions for biophotonic applications.

title: The NPC1L1 Sterol Transporter: A Molecular Dynamics Study on the Influence of Cholesterol Binding on Intradomain and Interdomain Motions.
authors: Ranaudo, Anna; Cosentino, Ugo; Greco, Claudio; Moro, Giorgio; Citterio, Sandra
journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
abstract: The Niemann-Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) transmembrane protein, localized on the apical membrane of enterocytes, is a key player in cholesterol metabolism and homeostasis, whose proper regulation is essential to avoid the development of cardiovascular diseases. The cryo-EM resolution of its structure in two distinct conformations provided a possible explanation of the mechanism which allows cholesterol to be transported from the lumen to the cytoplasm. This mechanism likely exploits the high mobility of the luminal N-terminal domain (NTD), which first binds the cholesterol molecule horizontal line although this was not resolved in the cryo-EM structures horizontal line  and whose spatial disposition with respect to the other extracellular domains is what most distinguishes the two conformations. In this work, we performed extensive all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the NPC1L1 protein, embedded in a membrane model, in four functional states: open apo, open bound, closed bound, and closed apo. Briefly, the analyses of the MD trajectories showed that the wide motions of NTD observed in the open apo state are partially restrained in the open bound state. Moreover, cholesterol binding to the NTD also makes this domain dynamically coupled to the collective rearrangements of the middle luminal domain (MLD) and the C-terminal domain (CTD). In the closed bound state, a new NTD-cholesterol hydrogen bond is observed, which could represent the first step for cholesterol delivery. Finally, the closed apo state is characterized by an increased MLD flexibility which may destabilize extracellular domain interfaces, preparing the NPC1L1 transporter to return to the open apo state. Ultimately, our protocol provides a robust framework that can be used to analyze novel NPC1L1 inhibitors.

title: Molecular Dynamics Investigation of Human Endosulfatase HSulf-2 Reveals the Structural Roles of Intrinsically Disordered Regions, Catalytic Residues, and N-Glycosylation.
authors: Tao, Jianjun; Daniel, Regis; Basdevant, Nathalie
journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
abstract: Human endosulfatases HSulf-1 and HSulf-2 are the only extracellular sulfatases that selectively remove 6-O-sulfate groups from heparan sulfate chains, thereby regulating numerous signaling pathways involved in development, tissue homeostasis, and cancer. In particular, HSulf-2 is frequently overexpressed in human cancers, making it an attractive therapeutic target. However, its three-dimensional structure has not been resolved experimentally, mainly because of its multidomain organization, extensive post-translational modifications, and large intrinsically disordered hydrophilic domain (HD). Here, molecular dynamics simulations based on the AlphaFold2 model of HSulf-2 were used to investigate the structural and dynamic contributions of its domains and selected post-translational modifications. The simulations identified several intrinsically disordered regions, confirming that the HD constitutes the principal source of conformational disorder within the enzyme. They further demonstrate that the CAT-Cter assembly reproduces the canonical catalytic architecture conserved throughout the sulfatase family, whereas the HD induces only minor changes in the average structure while significantly destabilizing the conformational dynamics of the catalytic framework. In contrast, maturation of the catalytic residue modulates the conformational landscape of HSulf-2 without altering its overall architecture, whereas the conserved chitobiose cores of N-glycans exert only limited structural effects. These results support a modular structural organization in which the CAT-Cter assembly provides the conserved catalytic scaffold, while the HD confers the dynamic properties required for recognition of polymeric heparan sulfate substrates. This work provides a structural framework for understanding HSulf specificity and opens new perspectives for the rational design of selective HSulf inhibitors. In particular, the modular organization suggests that future dual-site inhibitors that simultaneously target the conserved catalytic pocket and the unique hydrophilic domain could combine high binding affinity with selectivity for HSulf enzymes.

title: AlphaFold-based structural analysis of the Treponema pallidum proteome provides a clearer prediction of the organism's biological and pathogenic attributes.
authors: Kaval, Karan G; Parker, Emilio; Nguyen, Angelina; Brangulis, Kalvis; Edmondson, Diane G; De Lay, Bridget D; Norris, Steven J
abstract: Treponema pallidum subsp. pallidum (TPA), an obligate bacterial pathogen that causes the sexually transmitted disease syphilis, is an extreme auxotroph with a minimal genome and distinct parasitic lifestyle. Approximately 17% of its 977 annotated proteins lack a predicted function because they show little sequence similarity to proteins of known function from other organisms. We therefore utilized the robust structural modeling and matching capabilities of AlphaFold and FoldSeek to create a whole-proteome atlas for the Nichols type strain of this bacterium (TPANIC), with the goal of providing structure-based functional assignments for uncharacterized proteins and verifying the accuracy of annotations previously generated by protein sequence homology analysis alone. Using a combination of precomputed structures from the AlphaFold Database and newly generated AlphaFold 3 structural predictions, we produced high-confidence predicted structural models for approximately 92% of the TPANIC proteome, enabling us to identify structural homologs and assign potential functional annotations to 24 previously uncharacterized proteins. Beyond functional annotation, the updated genome-derived structural models revealed several major structural revisions resulting from corrected gene models. Most notably, integration of comparative structural analyses and AlphaFold-Multimer modeling redefined the composition of the TPA outer membrane biogenesis machinery, supporting the existence of a conserved spirochete-specific BAM-TAM complex containing BamA, TamB, BamD, and BamB. We anticipate that the resulting AlphaFold protein structure atlas, in combination with the recently developed tools of in vitro cultivation and genetic manipulation, will help elucidate the roles of TPANIC proteins in the organism's biology, pathogenesis, and host immune interactions.IMPORTANCEIncidence of syphilis has been on the rise in the past decade, emphasizing the need to understand the mechanisms behind the persistence and virulence of its causative agent, Treponema pallidum. In this study, we employed a next-generation artificial intelligence-based protein structure modeling and matching pipeline, building upon prior structural conservation studies by expanding the functional predictions for hypothetical proteins. Consequently, this study provides a clearer picture of the metabolic and pathogenic capabilities of this elusive pathogen, while highlighting the intricacies of its regulatory landscape. We anticipate that our strategy will complement existing sequence-homology-based gene/genome annotation pipelines, assisting in both protein function validation and the identification of orthologous proteins lacking sequence homology.

title: Beyond AlphaFold 3: a standardised benchmark of open-source co-folding models for antibody-antigen complexes, from docking accuracy to interaction specificity.
authors: Ramon, Aubin; Cheruku, Arnav; Zhao, Haowen; Sormanni, Pietro
abstract: Co-folding models are increasingly used to predict antibody-antigen complexes for epitope mapping, candidate triage and structure-guided de novo design or engineering, yet the latest generation of these models has not been compared under standardized conditions. We benchmark AlphaFold 3, Protenix-v2, ESMFold2, ESMFold2-fast and OpenDDE on 200 test-set complexes (121 Fvs and 79 V(H)Hs) from SAbDab2-Bench, a newly curated dataset, and a reconstructed antibody-antigen subset of FoldBench, Ab-FoldBench. Using standardized inputs, sampling, and interface metrics that isolate the antibody-antigen interface, we compare docking accuracy, inference-time scaling, confidence-based candidate structure selection and sensitivity to interaction perturbations. OpenDDE achieved the highest median DockQ and docking pass rate, followed by Protenix-v2, although their difference was not statistically significant. Both models outperformed AlphaFold 3 on these measures, alongside offering fewer licensing restrictions on model and prediction use. We further find that model confidence was generally effective at identifying accurate predictions but showed model-dependent variations. To probe interaction specificity, which is essential for antibody design, we generated decoys through non-conservative interface mutations, and non-cognate antigen shuffling. Confidence decreased for both perturbations, but more consistently for non-cognate antigens than for interface mutations, with OpenDDE retaining comparatively high confidence for many decoys. Overall, Protenix-v2 combined high docking accuracy with strong rejection of perturbed interfaces, OpenDDE achieved the highest docking accuracy, albeit at the longest runtime, while ESMFold2-fast offered the fastest inference for large-scale triage. These results provide an up-to-date guidance framework for selecting and configuring co-folding models in antibody discovery, design, and engineering.

title: [Exploration of the multi-target mechanisms of Shenju Yin in treating sperm DNA damage: An integrated study combining network pharmacology, molecular docking, and dynamics simulation].
authors: Fan, Qian; Chen, Shuo; Qian, Huaying; Zhao, Qi; Xue, Jianguo; Chen, Yun; Zhou, Yuan
journal: Zhonghua nan ke xue = National journal of andrology
abstract: Objective To explore the potential pharmacological targets and mechanisms of action of Shenju Yin, a formula derived from a renowned classic prescription, in treating sperm DNA damage (SDD) by integrating network pharmacology, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulation techniques. Methods Potential active ingredients of Shenju Yin were retrieved via the Traditional Chinese Medicine Systems Pharmacology Database and Analysis Platform (TCMSP) and the Bioinformatics Analysis Tool for Molecular mechanism of Traditional Chinese Medicine (BATMAN-TCM 2.0). Relevant target genes for SDD were identified by cross-referencing the OMIM and GeneCards databases. The Cytoscape 3.10.0 software was employed to construct and visually analyze protein-protein interaction networks and a "disease-target-gene" network. Molecular docking validation of core active ingredients with target protein structures was performed using AutoDockTools-1.5.7. The top three complexes with the strongest binding affinity from docking were subjected to molecular dynamics simulation using Gromacs (2025.2). Results Nine core active components were screened including quercetin, palmitic acid, myristic acid, stearic acid, benzoic acid, myrtenol, kaempferol, luteolin and octanol. Nine core targets including TP53, AKT1, JUN, ESR1, TNF, SRC, IL6, BCL2 and CTNNB1were identified , along with three key pathways such as the Hallmark of Cancer Cell Proliferation Persistence, Gastrin Signaling Pathway and Cancer Pathway. Validation demonstrated strong binding for three complexes: BCL2-luteolin, TP53-kaempferol, and BCL2-quercetin. Conclusion Shenju Yin may treat sperm DNA damage through a multi-component, multi-target, and multi-pathway synergistic mechanism characterized by "antioxidation, mitochondrial stabilization, and apoptosis inhibition." This study provides a scientific basis for the clinical efficacy of Shenju Yin and indicates directions for further experimental validation.

title: Protein engineering in Brazil: a biophysical perspective.
authors: de Lima, Mariana Zuliani Theodoro; Umbehaun, Gustavo Foltran; Tomazini, Atilio Jr
abstract: Protein engineering has become an increasingly interdisciplinary field, integrating molecular biology, structural biology, biophysics, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence to modify protein structure, stability, dynamics, molecular recognition, and catalytic activity. This systematic review examines the historical development and scientific contributions of protein engineering research associated with Brazilian institutions between 1988 and June 2026. A total of 792 peer-reviewed articles were identified in PubMed through eight thematic search strategies covering protein and enzyme engineering, directed evolution, rational and computational design, recombinant protein expression, therapeutic proteins, structural biology, and artificial intelligence-assisted engineering. The reviewed literature reveals a transition from early residue-level mutagenesis and conventional biochemical assays to increasingly integrated experimental and computational approaches. Advances in X-ray crystallography, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), circular dichroism (CD), mass spectrometry, small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), calorimetry, molecular dynamics, and structural bioinformatics enabled the quantitative investigation of protein folding, stability, conformational landscapes, molecular interactions, and catalytic mechanisms. More recently, machine learning, protein language models, AlphaFold-derived structures, and generative approaches have expanded the capacity to predict mutations and design proteins, peptides, antibodies, and enzymes with predefined properties. Overall, protein engineering in Brazil has evolved into a mature and diverse field with applications in health, infectious diseases, agriculture, biotechnology, bioenergy, biomaterials, environmental remediation, and industrial biocatalysis. The findings indicate that biophysics has moved beyond a predominantly descriptive role and has become central to the design and validation of engineered proteins. Future progress will depend on the convergence of experimental biophysics, multiscale simulations, artificial intelligence, high-throughput validation, and stronger national and international research networks.

title: CRAFT: an antigen-specific TCR generative model for conditional de novo design with physicochemical constraints.
authors: Yang, Xiaochuan; Li, Zaiduo; Li, Zhijuan; Zhang, Wei; Zhang, Xianyu; Yang, Tiansong; Liu, Mingliang; Li, Xiaokun
abstract: T-cell receptors (TCRs) are essential to adaptive immunity and mediate the recognition and elimination of malignant or infected cells through antigen-specific interactions. Despite the clinical progress of TCR-based immunotherapies, computational de novo design of antigen-specific TCRs remains difficult. The main difficulties include the complexity of peptide-major histocompatibility complex (pMHC)-dependent recognition, strict physicochemical requirements at the binding interface, and the small amount of paired training data available for model development. Current generative approaches depend largely on 1D sequence statistics and do not capture pMHC presentation context, interfacial physicochemical properties, and native receptor priors within a unified framework. We present conditional reconstruction of antigen fragments for TCRs (CRAFT), a decoupled generative model for pMHC-conditioned de novo design of antigen-specific TCR CDR3$\beta $ sequences under physicochemical constraints. With large-scale pretraining, CRAFT learns base representations that help reduce the limitations imposed by data scarcity. We further incorporate antigen-derived contextual information to guide antigen-specific TCR CDR3$\beta $ sequence design. The architecture comprises an antigen encoder (PrimeBERT) that captures the pMHC context and an autoregressive decoder (PrimeTCR) that preserves native receptor priors. The encoder and decoder are coupled through cross-attention and augmented with Atchley factor embeddings, allowing CRAFT to incorporate physicochemical constraints relevant to antigen-conditioned receptor design during sequence decoding. Across multiple evaluations, CRAFT demonstrates competitive sequence naturalness, together with favorable performance in specific binding, and predicted structural plausibility. Overall, CRAFT provides a computational framework for developing personalized tumor immunotherapies. It also holds potential to support clinical translation by enabling the efficient, targeted discovery of candidate TCRs.

title: CATH and TED in 2026: expansion in the number and diversity of CATH superfamilies.
authors: Edmunds, Nicholas S; Sillitoe, Ian; Miller, David; Waman, Vaishali P; Alvarez-Carreno, Claudia; Jones, David T; Bordin, Nicola; Orengo, Christine
abstract: CATH (https://www.cathdb.info) is a widely used bioinformatics resource that classifies protein structural domains from the wwPDB and integrates evolutionary, structural, and functional annotation alongside interactive visualization and analysis tools. CATH is recognized as a Core Data Resource by ELIXIR and a Global Core Biodata Resource by the Global Biodata Coalition. CATH continues to expand its coverage of protein structure space by integrating experimentally determined structures from the Protein Data Bank with the rapidly growing collections of predicted structures from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database as part of The Encyclopedia of Domains, the new sister resource of CATH. We provide an update on advances in new homology detection protocols and automated workflows providing end-to-end domain annotation and classification for processing large-scale protein structural data.

title: Transforming Neuroscience Research through AI-Driven Data Integration and Analysis.
authors: Gala, Rohan; Solanki, Arnav; Wang, Ning; Nikbakht, Nader; Warrell, Jonathan; He, Chenfeng; Huo, Bing-Xing; Ghosh, Satrajit; Xu, Hua; Hawrylycz, Mike; Jim Zheng, W
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Integrating multimodal data is essential to advance neuroscience as a discipline. Large-scale collaborative efforts, exemplified by the BRAIN Initiative, together with advances in single-cell and spatial omics, multimodal imaging, human genetics, behavioral phenotyping, protein structure prediction, and related technologies, are transforming neuroscience into a data-rich, highly interconnected science. As experimental resources, scientific literature, and collaborative networks continue to expand, integrating discoveries across modalities, species, and levels of biological organization has become the field's central bottleneck. This Perspective argues that artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming essential for overcoming these constraints. Using six evolving approaches we outline strategies to accelerate AI adoption through community building and pilot projects that drive AI transformation at both the organizational and technological levels. Organizational transformation cultivates broad AI awareness and a pro-AI culture while technological transformation improves the efficiency, scalability, and quality of data analysis, allowing researchers to generate insights more rapidly and effectively. Together, these advances position AI as a key driver for advancing neuroscience at scale.

title: Structurally Characterized Haloacid Dehalogenase 4A Catalyzes Fluoroacetate Defluorination and Provides a Scaffold for Exploring Organofluorine C horizontal line F Bond Cleavage.
authors: Hu, Miao; Bhardwaj, Shefali; Newton, Sophia; Caputo, Alessandro T; Manefield, Michael J; Scott, Colin
journal: Chembiochem : a European journal of chemical biology
abstract: Haloacid dehalogenases (HADs) catalyze hydrolytic carbon-halogen bond cleavage and are a tractable enzyme family for studying C horizontal line F bond cleavage. In this study, we characterized HAD 4A from Delftia acidovorans strain D4B. Recombinant 4A was expressed, purified, and crystallized, yielding a 1.59 A apo structure (PDB 9C9E) with an accessible aspartate (Asp22)-centered active site. Under the reported assay condition, purified 4A catalyzed hydrolytic defluorination of fluoroacetate, as supported by enzyme-dependent fluoride release and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry detection of glycolate. The docking model placed the fluoroacetate alpha-carbon near Asp22, providing computational structural context consistent with Asp22 acting as the putative catalytic nucleophile. Compared with related HAD-like dehalogenases, 4A showed a more open active-site entrance, suggesting a possible scaffold for organofluorine accommodation and structure-guided engineering. Exploratory reactions with PFOA (0.5 mM) and high 4A loading (500 microM, 120 h) produced only weak apparent fluoride release (~6 microM). These data do not demonstrate PFOA defluorination but identify 4A as a validated fluoroacetate-active HAD scaffold for future organofluorine biocatalysis.

title: A Thermostable GH29A alpha-L-Fucosidase from Thermotogaceae with Bifunctional Hydrolytic and Transfucosylation Activities: Computational Mechanistic Insights and Efficient Enzymatic Synthesis of 2'-Fucosyllactose.
authors: Hamouda, Hamed I; Chen, Changzheng; El-Sayed, Mohamed H; Nassar, Hussein N; El-Gendy, Nour Sh; Hashem, Amr H; Liu, Qishun; Qu, Jialin; Li, Tang; Yin, Heng
abstract: How GH29 alpha-L-fucosidases balance hydrolysis against transfucosylation at the structural level remains poorly defined, limiting rational engineering of these enzymes for glycoside synthesis. We report Thermo-Fuc, a thermostable GH29A alpha-L-fucosidase from a Thermotogaceae bacterium with an unusually alkaline pH optimum (9.0), a temperature optimum of 50 ℃, and a half-life beyond 6 h. The enzyme hydrolyzes diverse fucosylated substrates, favoring branched Lewis antigens (Leᵃ, Leˣ) over linear HMO backbones such as 2'-FL and 3-FL (K(m) = 1.015 mM, kcat = 0.00232 s(-)(1) for pNP-alpha-L-fucopyranoside), and under optimized conditions converts substrate to 2'-fucosyllactose at a 72.1% (mol/mol) transfucosylation ratio with high regioselectivity, confirmed by LC-MS and (1)H-NMR, among the highest yields reported for a wild-type GH29A enzyme. Sequence and structural analyses identified a conserved Asp219-Glu261 catalytic dyad, while molecular dynamics simulations revealed substrate-dependent flexibility across five active-site loops. The most catalytically productive complex had the lowest PC1 variance (17.4%) of all those tested, suggesting its activity depends on a broad, distributed range of active-site motions rather than a single dominant conformational switch. Together, these findings offer a testable, flexibility-based model of catalytic selectivity in GH29 fucosidases and mark Thermo-Fuc as a promising biocatalyst for enzymatic HMO synthesis.

title: Discovery of Novel Endolytic Hyaluronate Lyases Belonging to a New Subfamily of GH56 and Enhancement of Catalytic Activity through Catalytic Cleft Engineering.
authors: Yu, Xiangfan; Jing, Yiwen; Liu, Lei; Ma, Zhenyu; Jiang, Xukai; Xu, Li; Xiao, Min
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Hyaluronate lyases have been widely used to degrade hyaluronic acid (HA) and prepare HA oligosaccharides. To date, no hyaluronate lyase has been reported in glycoside hydrolase family 56 (GH56). Herein, SpskHL from Sporothrix schenckii 1099-18 was first identified as a GH56 endolytic hyaluronate lyase, and then its four homologues were discovered. These five microbial GH56 enzymes cleaved HA, yielding unsaturated HA oligosaccharides with DeltaHA2 as the end product, forming a new GH56 subfamily of endolytic hyaluronate lyase. Through alanine-scanning mutagenesis of 15 residues in the catalytic cleft of SpskHL and combining three positive mutations, triple-site mutant SpskHLM3 (Y120A/N125A/H189A) increased activity by 126%. Grafting of the triple-site mutation onto four other hyaluronate lyases increased their activities by 74%-155%. Molecular dynamics simulations suggested that all five triple-site mutants had an expanded catalytic cleft, a larger cavity near the catalytic residue E, and a shorter catalytic OE2-O4 distance, which might contribute to their enhanced activities.

title: Structural and Functional Characterization of the N-Prenyltransferase DsKabA in Algal Neurotoxin Biosynthesis.
authors: Huang, Wei-Jia; Chen, Sheng-Chia; Chien, I-Weh; Lin, Chia-Hsin; Zhou, Jia-Yi; Guo, Bo-Yan; Chang, San-Chi; Lin, Sheng-Wei; Hsu, Chun-Hua
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Kainic acid (KA) is a neuroactive natural product from the red alga Digenea simplex. Its biosynthesis begins with DsKabA, an N-prenyltransferase that converts l-glutamate and dimethylallyl pyrophosphate into prekainic acid, the first committed intermediate. Here, we combined LC-MS activity assays, X-ray crystallography, SAXS, molecular docking, ITC, MD simulations, and mutagenesis to characterize DsKabA. Product analysis confirmed prekainic acid formation, and kinetic measurements yielded apparent Km values of 1.03 +/- 0.16 muM for DMAPP and 52.25 +/- 1.61 mM for l-Glu. The 2.85 A apo structure revealed open and closed conformations involving the alpha7-loop-alpha8 region near the active site. Docking, ITC, and mutagenesis support Mg2+-dependent donor binding, ordered l-Glu association, and roles for Y403, H406, E407, M114, and M118 in catalysis and prenyl-donor recognition. These findings provide structural and mechanistic insight into the first committed step of KA biosynthesis.

title: Integrating Ion Mobility Mass Spectrometry Data with AlphaFold and Rosetta Improves Protein Complex Structure Prediction.
authors: Narayanasamy, Akshaya; Drake, Zachary C; Turzo, S M Bargeen A; Rolland, Amber D; Prell, James S; Wysocki, Vicki H; Lindert, Steffen
abstract: Ion mobility mass spectrometry (IM-MS) provides valuable structural information about protein shape and size through collision cross section (CCS). However, it lacks atomic level structural detail. While AlphaFold has been successful in predicting monomeric protein structure, it can struggle with modeling protein complexes. To address these limitations, we developed a method that integrates IM-MS data with AlphaFold and Rosetta to improve complex structure prediction. Our approach docks AlphaFold predicted subunits with Rosetta and selects the resulting models with a newly developed score that incorporates experimental or simulated CCS data. Using this strategy, we were able to improve normalized root mean square deviation (RMSD100) values for 26 of 38 (68%) complexes compared to AlphaFold-Multimer. Furthermore, 14 of these systems improved significantly from greater than 4 A RMSD100 to less than 4 A. This method demonstrates a robust approach to overcome limitations in complex assembly modeling.

title: peleke-1: A Suite of Protein Language Models Fine-Tuned for Targeted Antibody Sequence Generation.
authors: Santolla, Nicholas; Pridgen, Trey; Nigam, Prbhuv; Ford, Colby T
abstract: The discovery of therapeutic antibodies is a traditionally arduous process. Today, the lab-based process of antibody discovery consists of several time-consuming steps that involve live animal immunization, B-cell harvesting, hybridoma creation, and then downstream engineering and evaluation. However, the use of artificial intelligence in drug design has previously been shown effective in the rapid generation of protein-specific binders, small molecules, and even antibody therapeutics, thereby replacing some of the primary steps of the drug discovery process. Here, we present peleke-1, a suite of protein language models fine-tuned from state-of-the-art large language models using curated antibody-antigen complex data. These models generate targeted antibody Fv sequences for a given antigen sequence input at-scale. This suite of models provides a reliable, artificial intelligence-driven approach for in silico therapeutic antibody discovery along with an open-source framework for future antibody language model tuning.

title: Early Pathway Selection Precedes Conformational Locking in Protein Self-Assembly.
authors: Peng, Ruoxuan; Zhou, Lele; Bai, Runnan; Yang, Yunhao; Zhou, Yi; Zhang, Hao; Wang, Xinyan; Ren, Jing; Li, Jian; Liu, Yifan; Ling, Shengjie
abstract: When early intermediates begin to bias subsequent pathways during protein self-assembly remains difficult to resolve experimentally because early-stage processes are transient and poorly accessible. Here, using regenerated silk fibroin as a model system, we experimentally capture and analyze an early nucleation window in which assembly pathways begin to diverge before conformational locking occurs. By combining controlled electric-field perturbation with multiscale structural characterization and coarse-grained simulations, we identify reproducible nanoscale intermediates that mediate pathway selection. Within this window, electric fields bias early assembly kinetics in a nonmonotonic manner, modulating the formation, elongation, and competition of intermediates rather than directly enforcing structure or orientation. Time-resolved measurements show that subsequent growth proceeds primarily through elongation and fusion of existing intermediates, while beta-sheet formation and crystallization emerge only at later stages and serve to stabilize pathways that were biased at earlier stages. Together, we locate the emergence of detectable pathway biasing within the nucleation stage and provide a framework for understanding and guiding protein self-assembly under nonequilibrium conditions.

title: Development of reactive force field for Pd-Zn system and kinetic study of diffusion-driven alloy formation.
authors: Sun, Hongliang; Chen, Zhao-Xu
abstract: PdZn alloys are catalysts for many reactions, and the 1:1 tetragonal PdZn intermetallic compound has been identified as the active phase for methanol steam reforming (MSR), a crucial process in hydrogen production. Yet, the mechanism and kinetics of the formation of PdZn alloys have not been addressed theoretically. In this work, reactive force field (ReaxFF) parameters for the Pd-Zn system were developed using density functional theory (DFT) training sets generated with the aid of structure prediction and DFT calculations, and the alloying process of Pd and Zn metals was investigated by molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. MD simulations of Pd@Zn and Zn@Pd core-shell models revealed a two-stage, diffusion-controlled alloying process with distinct diffusion coefficients and activation energies for Pd and Zn atoms, and a kinetic model was proposed for the fast alloying stage. It is found that with the advance of alloying, the alloying activation energy of the rapid alloying stage increases, and it is also proportional to the cube root of the total atom number of the system. Simulations of a Zn/Pd(111) slab model further reproduced the experimentally observed temperature dependence of the surface alloy structure: a multilayer PdZn alloy at lower temperatures and a bilayer alloy at higher temperatures. The results provide valuable insights into the fundamental mechanisms of PdZn alloy formation and offer a robust foundation for further research in catalytic applications.

title: MARS: Machine-Learned Force Field Framework for Automated Conformational Sampling, Vibrational Spectroscopy, and Microsolvation.
authors: Suarez-Dou, Sergio; Gallegos, Miguel; Brunig, Florian N; Tkatchenko, Alexandre
journal: Journal of chemical theory and computation
abstract: We present MARS, an open-source Python package for automated conformational ensemble generation, infrared spectrum prediction, and explicit microsolvation of molecular systems. Built on JAX for GPU acceleration and automatic differentiation, MARS is carried out with machine-learned force fields (MLFFs), including SO3LR and MACE, with a four-phase conformational sampling workflow combining metadynamics, multitemperature molecular dynamics, and genetic algorithms. The package provides automated vibrational mode classification using Wilson B-matrix projections and functional group identification via graph-based pattern matching. We benchmark MARS on chemically diverse systems, including alkanes, halogenated aromatics, amino acids, peptides, drug-like molecules, phosphamides, host-guest complexes, and microsolvated biomolecular models. Semiempirical quantum-chemical methods have until now provided the practical state of the art for automated conformational sampling. Our benchmarks show that modern MLFFs can improve upon this paradigm by combining greater accuracy for high-level relative conformer energies with lower computational cost and more favorable scaling with molecular size. IR benchmarks against experimental gas-phase spectra additionally show performance comparable to quantum-chemical methods, with chemically interpretable mode assignments. Applications to alanine peptides, proline/beta-cyclodextrin inclusion complexes, alanine dipeptide, and 2-methoxycyclohexanone further demonstrate that MARS captures conformational reorganization, noncovalent binding motifs, solvent-induced stability shifts, and spectroscopic signatures. These results establish MARS as a transferable and accessible platform for ensemble-based molecular modeling with machine-learned potentials. MARS is freely available at github.com/tcpunilu/mars.

title: EZpred: Improving Deep Learning-Based Enzyme Function Prediction Using Unlabeled Sequence Homologs.
authors: Zhang, Chengxin; Liu, Quancheng; Freddolino, Lydia
abstract: Features extracted from sequence homologs significantly enhance the accuracy of deep learning-based protein structure prediction. Indeed, homolog-aware models such as AlphaFold generally produce more accurate protein structures compared to single sequence-based methods like ESMfold. In contrast, features from sequence homologs are seldom employed for deep learning-based prediction of the biological functions of a protein, such as Gene Ontology terms or Enzyme Commission (EC) numbers. Although a small number of models also incorporate function labels from sequence homologs, they cannot utilize features extracted from homologs that lack function labels. To address this gap, we developed EZpred, which is the first deep learning model to use sequence homologs by extracting their sequence features while ignoring any function labels. Starting with the target sequence and homologs identified by MMseqs2, EZpred extracts sequence features using the ESM-C protein language model. These features are then fed into a deep learning model to predict the EC numbers of the target protein. For test enzymes with < 30% sequence identity to any training proteins, the F1-score of EZpred EC number prediction is at least 34% higher than state-of-the-art EC number prediction models. These results demonstrate the strong positive impact of sequence homologs in deep learning-based enzyme function prediction.

title: Deep learning-based structure modeling of the Treponema pallidum proteome: Insights into pathogenesis and syphilis vaccine development.
authors: Houston, Simon; Marshall, Steven; Miller, Austin; Palkowski, Aleksander; Alfaro, Javier A; Cameron, Caroline E
journal: Protein science : a publication of the Protein Society
abstract: Treponema pallidum ssp. pallidum, the causative agent of syphilis, has a small proteome and encompasses numerous strains. Knowledge gaps remain in understanding the molecular mechanisms of pathogenesis of this bacterium, as well as the structure and function of the full complement of proteins encoded by T. pallidum. Here, an artificial intelligence-based structure-to-function modeling workflow was used to investigate the complement of proteins encoded by T. pallidum. High-confidence structure models were generated for 976 T. pallidum proteins, covering 99% of the proteome. Analysis of the generated models using the protein structure comparison server distance-matrix alignment (DALI) enabled high-confidence, structure-based functional annotation of 877 T. pallidum proteins, including 240 of the 323 proteins of unknown function encoded by this pathogen. Additionally, 63 putative pathogenesis-related proteins (PPRPs) and seven treponemal proteins with previously uncharacterized similarity to outer membrane proteins (OMPs) from Gram-negative bacteria were identified. A workflow for B cell epitope (BCE) prediction identified 1133 surface-exposed, host-facing potential epitopes in known and predicted T. pallidum OMPs, of which 90 were prioritized based on bioinformatic analyses, biophysical properties, amino acid sequence conservation, and previous protein expression data. This work provides insight into T. pallidum pathogenesis through structure modeling-based functional annotation, including characterization of proteins of unknown function. This study also informs syphilis vaccine design by identifying new potential T. pallidum OMPs, as well as host-facing regions of T. pallidum OMPs that have conserved amino acid sequences in globally circulating strains.

title: ThermoMutDB 2.0: semiautomated literature curation and structural enrichment of thermostability data for protein mutations.
