authors: Rodrigues, Gratchela Dutra; Clementino-Silva, Alisson; Brant-Ribeiro, Taffarel; de Mendonca, Maria Luiza Maciel; Zuccolotto-Guimaraes, Barbara; Dos Santos, Fernanda Elen Silva; Guimaraes, Ronison Alves; Ferreira, Valentina Gessinger; Ehlert, Maria Eduarda; Quintanilha-Peixoto, Gabriel; Rodrigues-Silva, Damares; de Menek, Gabriel Liston; Goulart, Lucas Mocellin; Silva, Danilo de Castro; Zadra, Vivian Ferreira; Goes-Neto, Aristoteles; Pires, Douglas Eduardo Valente; Kremer, Frederico Schmitt; Xavier, Joicymara Santos
abstract: Experimental measurements of protein thermodynamic stability are essential for understanding the relationship between protein structure and function, the molecular consequences of mutations, and their potential implications for protein malfunction and disease. However, extracting these data from the literature remains constrained by labor-intensive manual curation. Here, we present ThermoMutDB 2.0, a scalable framework for semiautomated literature curation and systematic structural enrichment. It introduces a major architectural redesign that integrates a large language model with rule-based entity recognition to identify and prioritize publications reporting experimentally measured effects of protein mutations on thermostability, while retaining expert validation as the final curation step. Complementing this literature-processing workflow, ThermoMutDB 2.0 systematically enriches curated mutations with mutant structural models, enabling interactive three-dimensional contextualization of experimentally derived thermodynamic data. Applied to the literature retrieved from January 1976 to the most recent search update in 2026, the pipeline screened 5,934 candidate publications and prioritized 254 for expert review, resulting in the incorporation of 102 articles and 1763 new entries. Rather than representing a simple expansion of database content, ThermoMutDB 2.0 establishes an extensible human-in-the-loop architecture in which automated literature triage, expert curation, and structural modeling operate as an integrated workflow. This redesign provides a sustainable foundation for continuous database maintenance and for linking experimental protein stability measurements with their structural context (available at http://thermomutdb.pathotrack.health/).

title: Quantum-accurate enhanced sampling and mini-protein folding through replica exchange for multiscale neural network potentials.
authors: Solazzo, Riccardo; Gordiy, Igor; Riniker, Sereina
abstract: Neural network potentials (NNPs) have emerged as efficient alternatives to computationally demanding quantum-mechanical (QM) methods. AMPv3-EE-BMS25 (short AMP-BMS) is an equivariant NNP designed for multiscale ML/MM simulations that captures directional and long-range interactions. In classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, enhanced-sampling techniques are applied to cross large energy barriers and improve convergence. Among those, replica exchange with solute tempering (REST2) is an efficient method that selectively scales solute interactions while keeping the bath temperature fixed, thereby reducing the number of replicas required. Here, we present a REST2-like algorithm compatible with multiscale ML/MM simulations. This algorithm is combined with AMP-BMS by exploiting the separability of its Hamiltonian into solute-solute, solute-solvent, and solvent-solvent contributions. We validate the REST2-AMP approach on several peptidic systems in explicit solvent and demonstrate folding of the mini-proteins chignolin and CLN025 from extended conformations. Thus, our REST2 approach for ML/MM enables access to biologically relevant timescales while maintaining near-DFT accuracy.

title: In Silico Assessment of SYNGAP1 Missense Variant Pathogenicity.
authors: Ali, Aliaa E; Otranen, Henna-Riikka M; Lehtonen, Jukka V; Courtney, Michael J; Pentikainen, Olli T; Postila, Pekka A
abstract: SynGAP, a critical regulator at the postsynaptic density, is associated with Alzheimer's disease, tumorigenesis, and most notably, SYNGAP1-related disorders (SRD), which manifests as autism, epilepsy, and cognitive impairment. SRD is likely primarily caused by SynGAP missense (SGM) variants, whose pathogenicity is difficult to confirm experimentally. To address this issue, a wide range of structure- and/or sequence-based as well as machine learning- and deep learning-based in silico predictors were benchmarked against clinically annotated SRD data. Folding stability calculations (e.g., Foldetta) and deep learning methods ESM1b and AlphaMissense showed the highest prediction accuracy under default settings. Applying optimized nondefault thresholds, especially with AlphaMissense, could further improve predictor performance. The predictions exhibited a strong structural pattern: Pathogenic variants were highly enriched within defined structural domains, particularly the GAP and PH domains, whereas variants located in nondomain and nonmotif regions were predominantly predicted to be benign. The verified phosphosites and predicted phase separation impacting variants occupy matching sections, including the protein's N-terminal region and the vicinity of putative SH3-binding motif in the disordered regions. Thus, these regions collectively could act as phase separation-promoting segments, complementing the protein's trimerization-coupled coiled-coil domain. Finally, the SynGAP Missense (SGM) server was presented to support SynGAP variant assessment. The SGM server integrates a Data Table with top-performing predictors, a 3D Viewer for structure-level assessment and AI-generated lay summaries for all variants arising from single-base substitutions, including those not yet observed in public databases.

title: Superionic Al horizontal line O horizontal line H Compounds With Unconventional Stoichiometries Under Extreme Planetary Conditions.
authors: Wang, Zifan; Shim, Ji Hoon; Kim, Duck Young
abstract: Extreme pressure and temperature induce novel chemical behaviors, including unconventional stoichiometries and superionic states. Here, by combining crystal structure prediction with first-principles calculations, we identify two unconventional stoichiometries in the ternary Al horizontal line O horizontal line H system, AlOH and AlH(3)O(4), which lie on the convex hull at 300 GPa. Representative formation reactions become thermodynamically stable above 65 and 245 GPa after including ZPE, respectively. Both compounds are wide-gap insulators and AlH(3)O(4) exhibits pronounced site-dependent charge differentiation between inequivalent oxygen environments under high pressure. Crucially, ab initio molecular dynamics simulations reveal protonic superionic transitions at elevated temperatures, where protons diffuse like a liquid through rigid Al horizontal line O sublattices. High-pressure and high-temperature dynamical-state diagrams further indicate that the solid, superionic, and liquid regimes overlap with conditions expected in deep planetary interiors, suggesting that they could play important roles in chemical behaviors inside planetary bodies. These findings significantly enrich the high-pressure phase diagram of Al horizontal line O horizontal line H system and provide valuable insights into chemical behaviors under extreme conditions.

title: Hydration water drives elastin's entropic elasticity.
authors: Cam, Metehan; Tarakanova, Anna
abstract: Elastin endows arteries, skin and lungs with elasticity, yet the molecular origin of its entropic recoil remains debated. Using multi-microsecond all-atom simulations of a representative elastomeric region of human tropoelastin, the monomeric precursor of elastin, we quantify protein conformational entropy, hydration-water entropy, and protein- and water-mediated interaction enthalpies during stretching. Protein conformational entropy decreases modestly overall, with heterogeneous local entropic responses governed by secondary structure and sequence context. In contrast, hydration water provides the dominant unfavorable entropic contribution because stretching recruits many water molecules from bulk into a persistently low-entropy first hydration layer. Stretching also disrupts favorable intra-protein interactions while strengthening protein-water interactions, producing opposing enthalpic contributions that largely compensate the entropic penalty. Together, these results support a hydration-coupled thermodynamic mechanism in which water is the dominant entropic contributor to elastin recoil within a strongly compensating enthalpy-entropy balance.

title: Transmembrane Domain Composition Reflects Subcellular Localization of SNARE Proteins.
authors: Baumann, Christian; Pulido-Quetglas, Carlos; Fasshauer, Dirk
abstract: Transmembrane domains (TMDs) anchor proteins within membranes of distinct composition and biophysical properties, necessitating adaptation to each membrane's unique environment. SNARE proteins, the core mediators of eukaryotic membrane fusion, provide an ideal system to study such adaptations: they are ubiquitous across Eukaryota, with paralogs localized to different compartments that have evolved independently to match their membrane context. Here, we combine statistical analyses of approximately 14 000 SNARE TMDs with MD simulations of 28 human SNARE TMDs to uncover how TMDs have adapted to distinct membrane environments. We identify a clear compositional dichotomy that separates SNAREs of the early secretory pathway (ER and Golgi apparatus) from those of the late secretory and endosomal pathways: early TMDs are enriched in bulky Phe residues, whereas late TMDs are dominated by smaller Ile residues. The larger Phe side chains likely enhance hydrophobic interactions in loosely packed ER and Golgi membranes, while Ile likely prevents disruption of the tight lipid-lipid packing in the plasma and endosomal membranes, potentially contributing to protein localization. TMD lengths derived from MD simulations differ from those inferred by sequence-based approaches and show limited variation across compartments. Together, these results reveal how variations in membrane composition shaped SNARE TMDs across eukaryotic compartments.

title: Multi-model prediction and comparative study of protein folding rates based on LASSO feature selection.
authors: Chen, Guanhong; Xiao, Liping; Yu, Mingzhou; Bai, Gongxun; Jiang, Zhouting
abstract: Accurate prediction of protein folding rates is essential for understanding protein dynamics. However, existing structural parameters show limited generalizability across two-state and multi-state proteins and are affected by multicollinearity. Here, LASSO regression was applied to a training set of 145 proteins to identify six structural features (L(eff), LRO, ACO, Sheet, H(nc), and P(beta)) from 12 structural parameters. These features were used to construct four machine learning models (RR, RF, SVM, and SSA-BP). Model performance was evaluated on an independent test set of 29 proteins, with bootstrap resampling used to assess performance uncertainty. On the full test set, RF achieved the lowest RMSE and MAE, whereas SSA-BP showed the highest correlation coefficient (R =0.9282). Folding-type-specific analysis revealed distinct model performance patterns between two-state and multi-state proteins. SHAP analysis further showed that the relative contributions of structural features varied across models and folding types, with L(eff), LRO, and ACO making substantial contributions. Overall, the proposed framework integrates feature selection, predictive modeling, and model interpretation, providing an interpretable approach for protein folding rate prediction.

title: Impact of training data on deep learning-based RNA 3D structure quality assessment.
authors: Adamczyk, Bartosz; Szachniuk, Marta; Antczak, Maciej
abstract: Accurate reference-free assessment of predicted RNA 3D structures is essential for large-scale RNA modeling, yet the impact of training data on deep learning-based quality predictors remains poorly understood. Here, we present a systematic cross-training analysis of three deep learning predictors for RNA 3D structure quality assessment, each originally developed on distinct training sets. By retraining each predictor on alternative (nonnative) datasets-including RNA3DQA, a new set created specifically for this project-and evaluating performance on independent RNA-Puzzles benchmarks, we systematically assess the relative contributions of model architecture and training data composition. Our results reveal pronounced differences in cross-dataset generalization, with predictors often performing better when trained on nonnative datasets than on their native ones. Notably, the impact of the training datasets varied across predictors, with RNA3DQA yielding the overall best accuracy and ranking stability results specifically for the ARES model. Native training sets yielded better performance for RNA3DCNN and lociPARSE. These findings demonstrate that the characteristics of the training data play a dominant, model-dependent role in shaping the performance and robustness of reference-free RNA 3D structure quality assessment methods. We conclude with practical recommendations for designing transferable training datasets and for benchmarking deep learning-based quality predictors in RNA structural bioinformatics.

title: Unveiling the anti-inflammatory potential of coumarin-based Schiff base derivatives through structural characterization and in vitro and in vivo biological evaluation.
authors: Hiremath, Arpita F; Ronad, Pradeep Kumar M; Menasinakai, Akshata S
abstract: BACKGROUND: Chronic inflammation contributes to several diseases, creating a need for effective anti-inflammatory agents. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to synthesize, characterize, and evaluate coumarin-based Schiff base derivatives for anti-inflammatory activity. METHODS: Ten coumarin Schiff base derivatives (SB-1 to SB-10) were synthesized by condensing 7-amino-4-methylcoumarin with substituted aromatic aldehydes. The compounds were characterized using FT-IR and (1)H NMR spectroscopy. In vitro activity was evaluated using the egg albumin denaturation assay. The most active compounds were assessed for acute toxicity and in vivo activity using carrageenan-induced paw edema in Wistar rats. Molecular docking was performed against COX-2 protein structures, and drug-likeness and ADME properties were predicted using SwissADME. RESULTS: SB-5 and SB-6 exhibited the highest in vitro activity, producing 82.65% and 73.46% inhibition of protein denaturation, respectively, at 250 microg/mL. At 200 mg/kg, SB-5 and SB-6 produced 46.02% and 41.29% inhibition of paw edemarespectively, whereas diclofenac sodium produced 66.90% inhibition at the dose evaluated. Both compounds were well tolerated in the acute toxicity study. Molecular docking indicated favorable interactions with COX-2 targets. SwissADME analysis showed compliance with Lipinski and Veber criteria and favorable gastrointestinal absorption and pharmacokinetic properties. CONCLUSION: SB-5 and SB-6 demonstrated promising preliminary anti-inflammatory activity and warrant further target-specific, pharmacological, pharmacokinetic, and toxicity studies to validate their potential for drug development.

title: A Competing C-Terminal beta-Turn Controls Frame-Dependent Stability of Collagen Triple Helices.
authors: Naha, Aritra; Ghosh, Amar; Sarma, Bani Kanta
abstract: Frame-dependent stability of collagen triple helices is well documented, but its structural origin remained unresolved. Here we identify a C-terminal beta-turn-like conformational state with intramolecular CO...HN contacts as the competing motif governing this behavior. In POG-frame collagen mimetic peptides, a C-terminal primary amide promotes this beta-turn-like state via transient intramolecular CO...HN contacts involving the proline carbonyl, reducing its availability for interstrand hydrogen bonding and perturbing terminal polyproline II geometry, directly opposing triple-helix assembly. N-methylation or esterification suppresses beta-turn formation, enhancing stability by up to 7.5  degrees C. Conversely, beta-turn formation is disfavored in the GPO frame, where the same terminal amide reinforces interstrand hydrogen bonding. Density-functional theory, NMR, X-ray crystallography, circular dichroism, and molecular dynamics establish this structural basis. Trends across 20-22 residue collagen-mimetic peptides confirm the mechanism arises from local C-terminal interactions, independent of length. These findings reveal how terminal hydrogen-bonding interactions encode competing conformations modulating peptide folding and supramolecular assembly.

title: SeqSol-FECS: An Integrated Deep Learning and Structural Modeling Framework for Protein Solubility Engineering.
authors: Guo, Qian; Zhou, Xiao-Ting; Zhou, Ren; Fang, Zhang-Rong; Shen, Qi; Xue, Ya-Ping; Zheng, Yu-Guo
abstract: Escherichia coli is widely used as a workhorse for heterologous protein expression. However, insoluble protein expression is frequently encountered. The mechanisms underlying protein solubility remain incompletely understood, limiting the effectiveness of current protein solubility engineering strategies. Here, SeqSol, a sequence-level solubility prediction model capable of prioritizing single-amino-acid substitutions through WT-mutant rescoring, was developed using 71,425 proteins. SeqSol achieved an accuracy of 75.8% and an AUC of 0.840 on an independent test set and correctly identified experimentally validated solubility-enhancing mutations from diverse proteins. To minimize the risk of activity loss, candidate mutation sites were prioritized according to conformational flexibility, relative solvent accessibility, and evolutionary conservation before solubility engineering. Using only 30 experimentally tested mutations, the resulting SeqSol-FECS framework increased the solubility of two industrial enzymes from 56.18% and 10.53% to over 95%, respectively, while maintaining their specific activities. SeqSol-FECS provides an efficient strategy for enzyme solubility engineering and biomanufacturing applications.

title: Design Trade-Offs between Target Binding and Self-Association Revealed by De Novo SARS-CoV-2 Binders.
authors: Carcelen, Lourdes; Penas-Utrilla, Daniel; Ferrero, Diego S; Ferrer-Orta, Cristina; Nadal, Marta; Colizzi, Francesco; Munoz, Juana C; Taules, Marta; Verdaguer, Nuria; Marcos, Enrique
journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
abstract: De novo protein binders have emerged as a powerful platform for molecular recognition, yet achieving high affinity while maintaining favorable biophysical properties remains a major challenge. Here, using the SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain (RBD) as a model target, we generated two de novo protein binder design campaigns that deliberately imposed different trade-offs between binding and monomeric behavior, and benchmarked them against a set of experimentally validated binders. Through integrated experimental and computational analyses, we show that binder design is constrained by two distinct failure modes that require different optimization strategies. None of the 22 original designs showed measurable binding to the RBD, with one class remaining monomeric but failing to achieve sufficient target binding, while the other had more competent binding interfaces but exhibited excessive surface hydrophobicity that promoted self-association. By integrating AlphaFold-based predictions, molecular dynamics simulations, docking analyses, and surface aggregation propensity (SAP) calculations, we establish complementary computational signatures that distinguish these failure modes and reveal their underlying structural determinants. Guided by these insights, we prospectively redesigned a representative failed binder by reducing noninterface hydrophobicity while preserving folding and binding interface quality. Experimental characterization by SEC-MALS, surface plasmon resonance, and circular dichroism confirmed that the redesigned variants were stable monomers and acquired low muM binding affinities. Together, our results define the mechanistic trade-offs between binding and self-association in de novo protein binder design and provide a framework for diagnosing and rationally overcoming common design failure modes.

title: Pharmacophore-Conditioned Diffusion Model for Ligand-Based De Novo Drug Design.
authors: Alakhdar, Amira; Poczos, Barnabas; Washburn, Newell; Cusack, Kevin
journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
abstract: Developing bioactive molecules remains a central, time- and cost-heavy challenge in drug discovery, particularly for novel targets lacking structural or functional data. Pharmacophore modeling presents an alternative for capturing the key features required for molecular bioactivity against a biological target. In this work, we present PharmaDiff, a pharmacophore-conditioned diffusion model for 3D molecular generation. PharmaDiff employs a transformer-based architecture to integrate an atom-based representation of the 3D pharmacophore into the generative process, enabling the precise generation of 3D molecular graphs that align with predefined pharmacophore hypotheses. Through comprehensive testing, PharmaDiff demonstrates superior performance in matching 3D pharmacophore constraints compared to ligand-based drug design methods. Additionally, it achieves higher docking scores across a range of proteins in structure-based drug design, without the need for target protein structures. By integrating pharmacophore modeling with 3D generative techniques, PharmaDiff offers a powerful and flexible framework for rational drug design.

title: Systematic Profiling of Encoder Architectures and Multimodal Embeddings in Protein Foundation Models Reveals Data Set-Driven Separability Regimes in Prediction of Allosteric and Orthosteric Binding Sites.
authors: Bazarova, Alina; Verkhivker, Gennady M
journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
abstract: Allosteric regulation represents a fundamental mechanism of protein function, yet distinguishing allosteric from orthosteric protein-binding sites remains a persistent computational challenge. While multimodal protein foundation models offer the potential to integrate complementary biological signals, including sequence, structure, functional annotations, and conformational dynamics, their performance determinants in allosteric binding site detection remain poorly understood. We introduce a unified computational framework for profiling multimodal protein foundation models across distinct binding site separability regimes. Rather than evaluating models solely by predictive accuracy, the framework combines systematic modality embedding ablations, encoder architecture comparisons, and variance decomposition to characterize how evolutionary, structural, functional, and dynamical information contributes to allosteric site discrimination. Using the OneProt multimodal model, we evaluate two complementary levels of multimodal integration: (a) encoder architectures that differ in the modalities incorporated during pretraining and (b) downstream combinations of pocket, sequence, and text embeddings used for classification. To systematically probe the determinants of model performance, we benchmark these configurations across four assembled data sets of protein complexes representing a spectrum of biological complexity and a range of structural, dynamic, and evolutionary contexts for orthosteric and allosteric binding sites. Through comprehensive embedding ablations, encoder architecture comparisons, and variance decomposition, we demonstrate that model performance is governed primarily by intrinsic data set properties rather than architectural complexity, with data set identity accounting for 63.7% of explainable variance. Across the data sets examined, we identify substantial differences not only in overall separability but also in the information accessible from different pretrained representations. Single-modality controls show that high predictive performance does not necessarily imply reliance on the explicitly provided pocket representation: depending on data set composition, substantial discrimination can already be obtained from sequence- or text-based multimodal representations. Within-protein comparisons nevertheless demonstrate that pocket-containing representations retain binding site-specific discriminatory information when protein identity and the associated sequence and text representations are held constant. At the encoder level, structural and molecular dynamics encoders provide the greatest benefit in intermediate and high separability settings. Example-level analysis further shows that combining data sets can reshape which binding sites are preferentially recognized. These findings establish that the success of multimodal foundation models depends critically on alignment between available modalities and the biological signatures that distinguish regulatory classes in each data set.

title: HEIWA: Hybrid Explicit-Implicit Water Attention Affects Force Field Accuracy in Structure-Based Protein Language Model ESM3.
authors: Ernest Ho, Ngai Hei; Yang, Chao Tung; Ng, I-Son; Chang, Jo-Shu
journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
abstract: Protein language models have achieved remarkable success in structure prediction and de novo design. However, their understanding of physical interactions remains limited. For structure-based models, we hypothesize that this limitation stems from the absence of explicit solvent modeling: water mediates hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic burial, and electrostatic interactions that govern protein thermodynamics and kinetics, yet current structure-based models treat proteins as if they exist in a vacuum. Using thermophilic protein classification as a proxy task for force-field awareness, per-residue logit mis-correlated with H-bonds as a destabilizing attribute and exhibits significant solvent-accessible surface area (SASA)-dependent error, despite high overall classification accuracy. These artifacts point to the water-protein interface as a source of systematic bias. To address this, we propose HEIWA (HybridExplicit-Implicit Water Attention), a novel attention module that injects solvent-mediated force-field information into static ESM3 residue embeddings via an all-query-to-all-key water-residue attention. Biophysics-guided model selection identifies configurations whose residue-level outputs are more consistent with the RMSF benchmark and selected biophysical attributes, while classification performance remains broadly comparable to the baseline. By forcing the model to predict the protein thermophilicity from the contributions of individual residues, HEIWA learns biophysical patterns that can be extended to SUPFAM absent from the training data set. HEIWA also largely preserves the embedding structure of ESM3. Molecular dynamics simulations show improved kinetic stability under thermophilic conditions, suggesting the potential to generate structures with greater kinetic stability. To our knowledge, this is the first study to incorporate explicit solvent encoding into a residue-resolution protein language model.

title: Drugging Pockets at the Surface of c-MYC Oncoproteins Revealed by Well-Tempered Metadynamics.
authors: Ge, Yanhong; Lu, Huixia; Marti, Jordi
journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
abstract: The MYC oncogene encodes a master transcription factor essential for regulating cellular homeostasis, growth, and metabolism. However, its deregulation is involved in up to 70% of human cancers, where it drives uncontrolled cellular proliferation. Structurally, MYC is characterized by an N-terminal transactivation domain and a C-terminal bHLHLZ domain critical for DNA binding and dimerization with MAX. Despite its clinical significance, MYC has remained historically "undruggable" due to its intrinsically disordered structure and the absence of traditional binding pockets. In this study, we combined all-atom Molecular Dynamics and well-tempered metadynamics simulations to map the conformational landscape of a MYC motif in aqueous ionic solution. The selected energy-minimized structures exhibit stable conformations and drugging pockets, providing structural foundations for targetting c-MYC. Furthermore, both the electrostatic potential and docking results for the obtained structure and the MYC inhibitor's 10074-G5 demonstrated excellent fit, highlighting its potential as a drug target. This inhibitor, introduced in several previously unpublished drugging pockets, maintained a steady binding to MYC over unbiased trajectories lasting 1 mus. These findings provide a previously uncharacterized structural foundation for the design of innovative therapeutic interventions, such as small-molecule inhibitors or peptides aimed at disrupting oncogenic MYC activity.

title: AlphaFold3 Pseudo-Ensembles Capture beta-Sheet Organization and Structural Diversity of Short Amyloidogenic Peptides.
authors: Peccati, Francesca
journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
abstract: Beyond predicting unique native globular protein structures, AlphaFold has been used to sample conformational diversity in globular proteins. Here, we asked whether this capacity can be transferred to amyloid fibrils formed by short peptides, despite the fundamental difficulties posed by their polymorphism, sensitivity to environmental variables such as pH and cofactors, limited evolutionary constraints, and underrepresentation of amyloids in structural databases. Using a comprehensive set of short amyloidogenic peptides, we show that sets of AlphaFold3 (AF3) models (pseudo-ensembles) are accurate predictors of parallel versus antiparallel beta-sheet organization, correctly assigning 112 of the 117 peptides for which a clear preference is predicted. Moreover, the simultaneous sampling of both organizations provides a signature of structural diversity, as shown for the polymorphic peptides MVGGVVIA and LYIQWL. Modeling of the precise steric-zipper architecture is less reliable and biased toward compact arrangements, while prediction in the presence of cosolvents and metal ions does not reproduce solvent-mediated interfaces or noncanonical coordination geometries. Thus, although AF3 does not fully capture the physicochemical complexity of amyloid assemblies, its pseudo-ensembles provide a rapid and useful approach for predicting beta-sheet organization and identifying amyloidogenic sequences with potential structural diversity.

title: Benchmarking Protein-Ligand Cofolding Models: Correct Ligand Placement Is Decoupled From Accurate Protein Conformation.
authors: Obendorf, Leon; Doering, Niklas Piet; Knaus, Petra; Wolber, Gerhard
journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
abstract: AI-driven cofolding models have become central tools for predicting protein-ligand complexes, yet it remains unclear whether the resulting structures recover the correct protein conformation or merely place the ligand plausibly within an otherwise mispredicted fold. Here, we benchmark four state-of-the-art cofolding models, AlphaFold3, RoseTTAFold3, Boltz-2, and Chai-1, and show that correct ligand placement is systematically decoupled from accurate prediction of the surrounding protein conformation. As test systems, we use kinases and Class A G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), families whose pharmacology depends on well-defined conformational states. To enable a prospective assessment, we evaluate complexes released after the training cutoffs of all tested models, together with one earlier nucleotide-bound structure as a control. We find that state-defining structural features, including kinase activation-loop, DFG/DYG geometries, and GPCR intracellular conformations such as ICL3, are frequently mispredicted even when ligand root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) is low. Cofolding adaptively remodels the orthosteric pocket around the bound ligand, but this local adaptation rarely propagates to the correct global conformation. Incorporating state-annotated templates and filtered multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) improves conformational recovery in some cases but has little effect in others, and model confidence metrics correlate with small-molecule placement but cannot report whether the local pocket geometry was recovered. Furthermore, while orthosteric ligand placement is generally reliable, the single allosteric complex in our set is misplaced by all models, even under explicit guidance. These results identify conformational decoupling as a fundamental limitation of current cofolding approaches across the systems evaluated, with direct implications for state-selective and structure-based drug design.

title: FlexENN: A Graph Neural Network for Binding Energy Prediction of Globular and Intrinsically Disordered Proteins.
authors: Irshad, Maryum; Ori-McKenney, Kassandra; Dima, Ruxandra I
journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) drive a large fraction of cellular signaling, transcription, and assembly through interfaces that often lack a defined geometry, making the prediction of their binding energies challenging for methods developed primarily for folded complexes. Here, we introduce FlexENN, an interface-focused message-passing graph neural network framework comprising two independently trained models: FlexENN-F for folded protein complexes and FlexENN-I for complexes containing a disordered partner. The FlexENN architecture constructs a local interface graph in which each residue node integrates the relative geometry, flexibility-related structural descriptors, and sequence information, allowing the network to learn structure-affinity relationships from a single resolved bound conformation. We also construct an IDP-containing dataset for training the FlexENN-I model. Benchmarked across folded complexes and IDP-containing systems, including tubulin-tubulin interfaces within microtubules (MTs) and MTs in complex with microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs), with reference binding affinity values extracted from our experiments, the models reproduce physically reasonable energetic profiles, including the stronger interdimer relative to the lateral MT interactions, while feature-ablation analyses reveal system-dependent contributions of selected descriptors to the predictions. More broadly, this work delivers an accurate, structure-aware approach to predicting binding free energies for complexes of folded protein and complexes that contain ordered or partially ordered IDP regions for which a sufficiently well-defined bound structure is available.

title: Geometric-Chemical Distance between Protein Surfaces.
authors: Swami, Himanshu; McBride, John M; Eckmann, Jean-Pierre; Tlusty, Tsvi
journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
abstract: Proteins recognize, bind, and catalyze through molecular surfaces, where geometry and chemical patterning determine interaction. Comparing these surfaces requires both a geometric-chemical distance and a correspondence that relates one complete surface to another. Here, we introduce IFACE (Intrinsic Field-Aligned Coupled Embedding). IFACE derives a symmetric geometric-chemical distance by optimizing a probabilistic coupling over intrinsic geometry, mean curvature, electrostatics, hydrophobicity, and hydrogen-bond propensity. The same coupling provides an explicit surface map. For molecular-dynamics conformers, IFACE distinguishes the same protein from distinct proteins more accurately than TM-distance and a Laplace-Beltrami spectral distance. A Jensen-Shannon distribution distance performs best in this binary identity test because aggregate surface-feature distributions already identify each protein. A distance must also satisfy a global requirement: Its pairwise values must place many distinct protein surfaces consistently in one space. We therefore tested IFACE across six protein families. It produces the strongest family classification and clustering among the distributional, spectral, MaSIF, and SurfaceID comparisons. The inferred maps preserve geodesic neighborhoods and transfer heme-centered pocket regions across cytochrome P450 proteins. IFACE therefore provides, from one construction, both a distance between complete protein surfaces and the local map that explains that distance.

title: Mutations in the nsP1 dodecamerization surface impair Semliki Forest virus RNA synthesis in mosquito cells.
authors: Xin, Qilin; Kavil, Siji; Konno, Melis N; Anderson, Michelle A E; Alphey, Luke
abstract: Positive-sense RNA (+ssRNA) viruses remodel host membranes to form replication organelles (ROs), a process largely driven by the oligomerization of virus-encoded membrane-binding proteins. In the case of Togaviruses, non-structural protein 1 (nsP1) assembles into dodecameric rings that serve as scaffolds bridging viral replication spherules with the host plasma membrane. However, the precise role and necessity of nsP1 oligomerization in viral replication remain incompletely understood. In this study, we employed structure-based computational modeling to design nsP1 mutants predicted to disrupt monomer-monomer interactions within the dodecamer. Molecular dynamics simulations further indicated that these mutations may impair the membrane-binding affinity of nsP1. Western blotting was performed under denatured reducing conditions, and confocal microscopy was used to assess the expression levels and subcellular localization of mutant nsP1, respectively. Mutant proteins appear to not be stably retained at the plasma membrane, instead being mislocalized to endosomal compartments. Three-component trans-replicase assays and viral challenge experiments revealed that nsP1 dodecamerization-surface mutants are deficient in their ability to support viral replication. This study highlights the critical role of nsP1 dodecamerization in Togavirus replication and proposes a potential antiviral strategy targeting oligomeric protein structures in +RNA viruses. IMPORTANCE: Togaviruses are emerging arboviruses capable of causing severe disease and sporadic outbreaks. During viral replication, viral nsP1 assembles into dodecameric rings that anchor replication organelles called spherules to host membranes; however, the functional necessity of the oligomeric organization remains poorly defined. In this study, we combined structure-based modeling, molecular dynamics simulations, and cell-based assays to investigate how mutations that are predicted to destabilize nsP1 oligomers affect viral replication. We found that these mutations reduced membrane-binding affinity, altered subcellular localization, and nsP1 harboring these mutations failed to support viral RNA replication. These findings indicate that nsP1 dodecamerization is required for its stabilization on plasma membranes. More broadly, our findings suggest that targeting the oligomerization of membrane-associated replication proteins represents a viable antiviral strategy for Togaviruses and potentially other positive-sense RNA viruses.

title: Distinct roles of monosaccharides in the inhibition of the carbohydrate-binding module and catalytic domain of Cel7A.
authors: Pereira, Ander F; Martinez, Leandro; Skaf, Munir S
journal: Protein science : a publication of the Protein Society
abstract: The enzymatic breakdown of lignocellulosic biomass is a critical step toward the sustainable production of biochemicals. The cellobiohydrolase Cel7A plays a key role in this process by hydrolyzing cellulose. Both the primary reaction product (cellobiose) and secondary monosaccharides (glucose, mannose, and xylose) inhibit Cel7A's activity by interacting with its carbohydrate-binding module (CBM) and catalytic domain (CD). Previous works have established that while glucose directly slows the enzyme's catalytic rate (k(cat)), mannose and xylose primarily reduce its association rate (k(on)) and overall processivity. To uncover the microscopic mechanisms behind these observations, we employed all-atom molecular dynamics simulations combined with the Kirkwood-Buff solution theory. Our results reveal an unsuspected contrast in the solvation preferences of the two domains: while sugars are preferentially excluded from the CD, the CBM exhibits preferential sugar binding. We observed a high density of sugars along the CBM's planar binding face (residues Y5, Y31, and Y32), as well as near I11, S14, S21, V27, L28, and P30. Xylose, the most potent experimental inhibitor, displays the highest density near the CBM residues comprising the cellulose-binding face, which could interfere with the enzyme's anchoring of cellulose. Furthermore, we observed sugar accumulation at the entrance of the CD tunnel and within the tunnel-binding loops (B2, B3, and A3), providing a structural explanation for the obstruction of the enzyme's processive cycle. By reconciling broader solvation preferences with highly specific site interactions, our findings offer a picture of how glucose and hemicellulose-derived sugars inhibit Cel7A.

title: Molecular basis of ACE2 inhibition by the peptide DX600 revealed by computational and biophysical analysis.
authors: Mossa, Alessandro; Papalini, Alessia; Pacifico, Salvatore; Albanese, Valentina; Demo, Alfredo Garzino; Perris, Roberto; Rossi, Silvia; Tozzini, Valentina; Brancolini, Giorgia; Sgarbossa, Antonella
journal: Protein science : a publication of the Protein Society
abstract: This study investigates the molecular mechanism of Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme 2 (ACE2) inhibition by the peptide DX600 using an integrated computational and biophysical approach. Small molecules and peptides have been explored as ACE2 antagonists, including MLN-4760 and the peptide DX600, but the molecular determinants underlying their inhibitory mechanisms remain incompletely understood. MLN-4760 is known to interact within the catalytic cleft of ACE2 thereby inducing structural changes in ACE2 causing the receptor to undergo a transition from opened to closed conformation. On the contrary, our molecular dynamics simulations reveal that DX600 binding stabilizes the receptor, dampening fluctuations of key residues such as to lock the receptor in an open conformation. This stabilization produces a more rigid ACE2 structure, consistent with steric hindrance that may impede viral protein, for example, the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, engagement. RMSF analysis, which quantifies local structural fluctuations at the residue level, confirms that DX600 reduces local residue mobility, highlighting a distinct mechanism from small-molecule inhibitors. These results provide a detailed molecular picture of peptide-mediated ACE2 inhibition and offer insights for the rational design of ACE2-targeted small molecule therapeutics.

title: A cryptic binding pocket regulates the metal-dependent activity of Cas9.
authors: Ahsan, Mohd; Knight, Alexa L; Saha, Aakash; Ramos, Delisa; Strohkendl, Isabel; Skeens, Erin; West, Madeline S; Luo, Jinping; Dresser, Charlotte S; Taylor, David W; Lisi, George P; Palermo, Giulia
abstract: Cas9 is a metal-dependent nuclease used for genome editing across diverse cells and organisms exhibiting distinct ionic environments, yet how metal ions regulate its catalytic function, and consequently its editing efficiency remains unclear. Here, molecular simulations, Markov state models, and mixed quantum-classical approaches reveal that divalent metals promote activation of the catalytic HNH domain through formation of a divalent metal-binding pocket (DBP) at the HNH-RuvC interface. This cryptic pocket emerges dynamically during HNH activation and is supported by NMR measurements revealing metal-dependent structural perturbations within the HNH-L2 region. Mutations targeting the DBP disrupt HNH activation and impair the coupled catalytic activity of both nucleases, identifying the pocket as a key regulator of Cas9's metal-dependent activity. Together with quantum-classical simulations revealing distinct catalytic behaviours among divalent metals, these findings uncover an ion-dependent regulatory mechanism in Cas9 with insights for genome editing across diverse biological environments.

title: Distance-AF Multimer: A Multi-Step Approach for Protein Complex Structure Modeling with User-Defined Distance Constraints.
authors: Ling, Kai; Zhang, Yuanyuan; Zhang, Zicong; Nakamura, Tsukasa; Kihara, Daisuke
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: The three-dimensional structure of proteins provides essential insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying their function. Many biological activities are mediated through protein interactions, making accurate structural determination of protein complexes important. Despite significant advances in computational protein structure prediction, there are still many cases where protein complexes are not correctly assembled. In particular, there are cases where experimental data, such as distances between residue pairs in interacting proteins are available, yet existing prediction methods fail to produce models consistent with these data. Here, we present Distance-AF Multimer, a method that guides and refines AlphaFold-Multimer docking predictions using user-provided residue pair distance information. This approach extends our previously successful data-guided single-protein modeling method, Distance-AF. Distance-AF Multimer operates in a two-step process, starting from multiple initial conformations and iteratively refining them to satisfy the provided distance constraints. We evaluated Distance-AF Multimer on protein-complex benchmarks spanning different chain counts and docking errors, demonstrating competitive or superior performance compared to other existing deep-learning-based structure prediction methods. In addition to dimer cases, we also demonstrated the potential of Distance-AF Multimer for large-scale protein assemblies containing multiple chains, including those with more than 5 chains. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: Proteins often function as complexes, but predicting how their components fit together remains difficult. Distance-AF Multimer uses distance constraints between residues to improve the arrangement of protein chains in predicted structures. This approach offers a practical way to combine computational predictions with available structural information, helping researchers study protein interactions, peptide binding, and larger assemblies when detailed experimental structures are unavailable.

title: Edge-Aware Graph Attention Networks for Interpreting Biophysical Mechanisms from Molecular Dynamics Simulations.
authors: Ahsan, Mohd; Pindi, Chinmai; Rodriguez, Larry; Shah, Paaras; Palermo, Giulia
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Graph attention networks (GATs) are emerging as powerful aritficial intelligence (AI) tools for learning biomolecular dynamics, yet extracting mechanistic insight from learned attention remains challenging. Here, we present an interpretable AI approach that combines molecular dynamics prediction with mechanistic interpretation through attention-derived communication networks. We develop three edge-aware GAT models - Edge-Conditioned, Edge-Injected, and Edge-Gated - that differ in how edge information is incorporated during message passing. Relative to a standard GAT, our edge-aware models improve coordinate prediction while recovering complementary aspects of residue communication. Application to Chignolin and HIV-1 protease demonstrates their ability to characterize communication networks underlying protein folding, allostery, and mutation-induced functional remodeling. Analysis of the communication networks using graph-based descriptors of communication throughput, intensity, and relay revealed that the Edge-Conditioned model preferentially emphasizes communication hubs characterized by high communication throughput and intensity, the Edge-Injected model preferentially highlights high-intensity communication within functionally important regions, and the Edge-Gated model most clearly resolves long-range communication relay. Overall, this approach provides an interpretable AI strategy for uncovering the communication mechanisms that underlie folding, allostery, and long-range signal propagation in molecular machines, while also supporting AI-guided modulation of biomolecular function and rational protein engineering.

title: Structure-Based and Glycosylation-Aware Interpretation of Glycogene Variants.
authors: Ohno, Shiho; Manabe, Noriyoshi; Kaname, Tadashi; Nishihara, Shoko; Yamaguchi, Yoshiki
abstract: Missense variants in glycan-related genes (glycogenes) underlie many congenital disorders of glycosylation and related conditions, yet a large fraction remain classified as variants of uncertain significance. Because glycogenes often show low evolutionary conservation, conventional sequence-based predictors are frequently uninformative, making structure-based interpretation particularly valuable. This review examines how structure-based and glycosylation-aware approaches can improve the interpretation of glycogene variants. Advances in protein structure prediction, notably AlphaFold, now allow variant-induced structural perturbations to be assessed proteome-wide using structure-derived features such as solvent accessibility, thermodynamic stability (DeltaDeltaG), and local model confidence (pLDDT). Such structural features can be combined to predict the impact of glycogene variants, as exemplified by VarMeter and VarMeter2, which have successfully identified pathogenic missense variants of arylsulfatase L (ARSL) and N-sulfoglucosamine sulfohydrolase (SGSH) in patients with undiagnosed disease. Despite the progress in these tools, there remain challenges especially relevant to glycobiology, including the limited accuracy of current DeltaDeltaG predictors, the distinct behavior of gain-of-function and stabilizing variants, the need for proteome-scale computation, and the critical but still underexplored contribution of protein glycosylation to structural stability. We argue that incorporating glycosylation into structural energetics is a key next step toward more accurate, glyco-aware variant interpretation.

title: Messenger RNA vaccine platforms from molecular optimization to infectious disease and cancer immunotherapy: a narrative review.
authors: Wang, Qian; Sun, Zhangzhang; Liu, Heyong
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines now encompass licensed respiratory vaccines, a self-amplifying ribonucleic acid (RNA) product, and individualized cancer immunotherapies in late-stage development. The expansion of the field has made platform-level comparisons increasingly important because efficacy, tolerability, manufacturability, and tissue targeting are influenced by the RNA architecture as well as by the delivery system. This narrative review examines molecular engineering, delivery, emerging RNA architectures, infectious-disease translation, and cancer immunotherapy, with emphasis on developments reported through 2026. METHODS: Targeted literature searches were conducted in PubMed through 31 August 2026, complemented by reference chaining and targeted searches of official regulatory sources. English-language mechanistic studies, clinical trials, regulatory documents, and focused reviews were prioritized. Particular attention was given to evidence published from 2023 to 2026 on self-amplifying RNA (saRNA), circular RNA (circRNA), molecular optimization, and individualized neoantigen vaccines. KEY CONTENT AND FINDINGS: Nucleoside-modified non-replicating mRNA formulated in lipid nanoparticles remains the most clinically validated architecture. Molecular optimization now extends beyond nucleoside substitution to cap chemistry, untranslated-region selection, coding-sequence and RNA-structure design, poly(A) control, and removal of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) impurities. saRNA has reached regulatory authorization and offers dose-sparing potential, whereas circRNA remains predominantly preclinical and still faces unresolved manufacturing and quality-control questions. Infectious-disease programs have established reusable capabilities in antigen design, lipid nanoparticle formulation, manufacturing, and regulatory comparability. In oncology, intismeran autogene plus pembrolizumab has produced durable recurrence-free survival (RFS) benefit in resected melanoma, while pancreatic-cancer studies of autogene cevumeran show that vaccine-induced T cell responses vary substantially between patients. Tumor clonality, neoantigen quality, antigen presentation, the immune microenvironment, treatment setting, and manufacturing time are therefore as important as the number of encoded mutations. Artificial intelligence (AI) can improve neoantigen ranking but does not remove the need for biological validation. CONCLUSIONS: No RNA architecture is uniformly superior across indications. Further clinical progress will depend on matching transcript design and delivery to the intended immune response, improving predictive antigen selection and patient stratification, and transferring validated manufacturing and regulatory capabilities from infectious-disease vaccines to individualized oncology without assuming that platform maturity alone is sufficient for antitumor efficacy.

title: Predicting the alternative conformation of a known protein structure based on the distogram of AlphaFold2.
authors: Li, Jiaxuan; Zhu, Zefeng; Song, Chen
abstract: AlphaFold2 (AF2) has become one of the most established and leading tools for predicting protein structures, although it often favors a single conformation. While it has been shown that sampling different conformations is possible by manipulating the multiple sequence alignment (MSA), the potential for multi-state information within a standard AF2 prediction remains underexplored. In this work, we demonstrate that even with a deep MSA, AF2 predictions encode structural heterogeneity. Specifically, we observe that the predicted residue-residue distance distributions often exhibit multiple probability peaks before recycling, suggesting the presence of alternative states. We derive state-specific distance restraints by fitting and separating these multi-peak distributions. These restraints are then incorporated into Rosetta as energy terms to model large-scale conformational transitions. Across multiple protein systems undergoing diverse types of conformational changes, our method effectively samples alternative conformations starting from an input conformation, producing models comparable to those from existing approaches. Our findings highlight a previously underutilized feature of AF2 predictions and offer a novel strategy to take advantage of these insights to study conformational flexibility and dynamics in proteins. This work broadens the applicability of AF2 in structural biology and the modeling of multi-state protein systems.

title: Functional architecture of rare protein coding variation across 786,871 exomes.
authors: Hou, Kangcheng; Li, Hui; Nason, Emily; Finucane, Hilary; Sunyaev, Shamil; O'Connor, Luke J
journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
abstract: Protein coding variants span the gamut of structural and functional effects on proteins, and they have similarly heterogeneous effects on traits. Their functional effects can be predicted and categorized, particularly using machine learning models, and integrating these predictors benefits gene discovery. However, it remains unclear how well known structural features and predicted functional scores explain the heterogeneous effects of protein coding variants on human complex traits. We introduce the Kernel Allelic Series Model (KASM), which integrates multiple functional annotations to form a kernel describing how allelic effects within a gene covary. We apply it to exome data from 26 traits and 786,871 individuals from UK Biobank and All of Us, integrating 35 annotations describing protein structure and predicting allelic effects. We estimate that rare missense heritability is at least 1.27+/-0.09% on average, 1.83+/-0.11% under our most flexible model, exceeding pLoF heritability (0.87+/-0.05%) and far exceeding missense burden heritability as previously estimated (0.54+/-0.04%). AlphaMissense is the single most enriched missense predictor, but a composite score doubles its enrichment. A series of structural features is enriched for heritability, from amino acid chemical features and structural motifs to residue contacts and protein-protein interaction interfaces. Examining pairs of variants, we find that most missense effects are modestly correlated, but an exception is when residues are close in 3D structure but distant in 1D sequence; such pairs also covary across species. Finally, we analyze individual genes and identify gene-specific enrichments, like a 95-fold enrichment among PIEZO1 hydrogen bond residues, that nominate functional hypotheses.

title: Reliable and Efficient Agentic Protein Design with Toolset Harnessing.
authors: Butcher, Jasper; Chen, Jie; Hunt, Andrew; Haas, Cyrus M; Dai, Wenzhao; Sharma, Shajesh; Mitra, Raktim; Salike, Saman; Koob, Jeremy; Muraishi, Aiko; Li, Zhe; Pyles, Harley; Tyka, Michael D; Bauer, Magnus S; Brent, Rafi I; Mittal, Anant; King, Neil P; Baker, David
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Computational protein design workflows require the orchestration of multiple tools, data formats, and analysis steps that are often fragmented. Here, we introduce Chaperone, a lightweight and customizable framework that enables seamless integration of RFdiffusion3 (RFD3) [1] with downstream sequence design, structure prediction, and evaluation tools, including ProteinMPNN [2], AlphaFold3 (AF3) [3], and more than 50 other protein design tools. By combining a programmable agent-friendly interface with parallelized execution on high-performance computing systems, Chaperone as a harness enables rapid iteration and scalable exploration of complex protein design workflows. Across an evaluation of nine biomolecular design tasks, we find using Chaperone reduces total token usage relative to baseline agents by 86% and GPU costs by 64%, while increasing the overall computational design pass rate. We demonstrate Chaperone's utility for large-scale design-space exploration through a two-week end-to-end small-molecule binder design campaign, yielding low nanomolar binders to cortisol zero shot. We further demonstrate its versatility across distinct design challenges, including the design of a symmetric 12-subunit self-assembly nanoparticle and a linker that mediates interactions between C2- and D3-symmetric protein complexes to form crystalline assemblies. Together, these results demonstrate how agent harnesses built around standardized tool interfaces can substantially improve the efficiency and success of complex, long-horizon agentic design workflows in biology. We make Chaperone freely available to the community on GitHub: https://github.com/RosettaCommons/chaperone .

title: HV-MultiScaleGNN: A Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network Framework for Host-Virus Protein-Protein Interactions Prediction
authors: Sarangthem Dinamani Singh; Gori Sankar Borah; Selvaraman Nagamani
abstract: Accurate identification of HV-PPIs is essential for understanding viral infection mechanisms and for developing antiviral therapeutic discovery. However, the experimental identification process is often time-consuming and expensive, while many computational approaches depend on incomplete protein sequences, structural and interaction information. Here, we present HV-MultiScaleGNN, a topology-driven multi-scale GNN framework for HV-PPIs prediction that operates exclusively on the topology of a heterogeneous interaction network. The framework formulates HV-PPIs prediction as a heterogeneous link prediction problem by integrating the human interactome with experimentally validated HV-PPIs. HV-MultiScaleGNN systematically investigates three complementary graph representation strategies, viz. Local view, Global view and an integrated Local+Global view. The Local view employs one-hop relation-aware graph attention to model fine-grained neighbourhood interactions. The Global view captures higher-order structural dependencies through propagation-based neighbourhood aggregation. The integrated representation combines both views to jointly encode local connectivity and global topological context within a unified embedding space, enabling relation-specific link prediction without relying on sequence- or structure-derived features. Experiments on large-scale HV-PPIs datasets evaluate all three strategies using discrimination, calibration, and ranking metrics. The Local view achieved the best discriminative performance (AUROC = 0.9444, AUPRC = 0.9422), whereas the Global view exhibited the lowest ECE (0.0379). The integrated Local+Global view provided consistently strong predictive performance (AUROC = 0.9378, AUPRC = 0.9356). Comparative evaluation against representative graph representation learning methods showed competitive predictive performance. Furthermore, interfacial interactions were identified using protein-protein docking and atomistic-level understanding was explored. Moreover, GO and KEGG enrichment provided additional functional insights into the selected host proteins. The proposed framework enables systematic evaluation of complementary graph representation strategies for heterogeneous biological link prediction and helps experimental researchers to delineate novel HV-PPIs.

title: DynamicsPLM: A Dynamics-Enriched Small Protein Language Model for Protein Variant Effect Prediction
authors: Tuan Minh Dao; Amarda Shehu; Anowarul Kabir
abstract: Predicting how mutations impact protein function and stability remains a key challenge in computational biology. Current state-of-the-art protein language models (PLMs) primarily scale parameter size on sequence corpora to capture evolutionary constraints but remain blind to the explicit physical dynamics of folded proteins. Conversely, models trained strictly on physical dynamics neglect critical evolutionary sequence statistics. In this paper, we bridge this gap by introducing DynamicsPLM, a highly parameter-efficient 35-million-parameter model that unifies evolutionary and biophysical representation learning. Utilizing a second-stage, multi-task continual pretraining strategy on over 60,000 proteins, we enrich a foundational sequence encoder with explicit residue-level and pairwise molecular dynamics heads while preserving its original evolutionary knowledge. At inference, DynamicsPLM computes zero-shot mutation effects from sequence alone by balancing an evolutionary plausibility score against a structural dynamics disruption score. Across the massive ProteinGym benchmark and natural variants of the Tsuboyama folding stability dataset, DynamicsPLM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among all models under 100M parameters, and matches or outperforms several billion-scale sequence-based models of its size. Our findings demonstrate that explicit structural-dynamics supervision provides a parameter-efficient alternative to raw scale. Availability: All codes including data preparation scripts, training and validation recipes, and experimental configurations for LoMuS are available at: https://github.com/kabir-ai2bio-lab/DynamicsPLM.

title: Integrating evolutionary and protein language model representations for thermodynamically consistent stability prediction
authors: Guido Barducci; Tiziana Sanavia; Piero Fariselli
abstract: At fixed thermodynamic conditions, protein stability changes obey reversal antisymmetry and path independence, but learned predictors need not satisfy these properties. Explicit alignment-derived evolutionary information may also complement single-sequence protein language model representations, motivating their integration under clearly defined physical constraints. Here, we develop a training-free strategy that combines thermodynamic constraints with complementary sequence representations. We first introduce EvoPhi-DDG, a potential-based adaptation of the alignment-conditioned evolutionary predictor MSAesm_ddG. By antisymmetrizing its predictions and setting the hidden biases to zero, we express stability changes as differences of a learned, evolution-informed effective potential conditioned on the mutation site and alignment context. This guarantees exact reversal consistency and exact same-site transitivity under fixed alignment contexts while preserving predictive accuracy. We further extend the adapted predictor to multiple substitutions through a background-aware construction that preserves whole-variant antisymmetry. We then combine EvoPhi-DDG with the previously published JanusDDG using fixed, equal-weight averaging to test predictive complementarity without additional training. The ensemble preserves exact antisymmetry and reduces multisite pathway-closure RMSE relative to JanusDDG across all evaluated path lengths. Furthermore, the ensemble outperforms both components on S669 and S96, achieving Pearson correlations of 0.59 and 0.55, respectively, compared with 0.55 and 0.52 for JanusDDG and 0.53 and 0.48 for EvoPhi-DDG. On the multiple-substitution benchmark PTmul-NR, the ensemble achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.66, improving on JanusDDG’s 0.61 and matching the EvoPhi-DDG extension at the reported precision. Together, these findings distinguish two benefits: averaging complementary predictions improves accuracy, whereas the potential-based reformulation strengthens physical consistency. They support the integration of alignment-conditioned and single-sequence representations without additional training, while separating predictive improvements from mathematical guarantees.

title: Beyond Global Contrasts: Paired-Unit Activation Steering for Context-Aware Protein Sequence Design
authors: Yingtong Zhou; Xiaoning Qian; Byung-Jun Yoon
abstract: Activation steering in protein language models enables controllable sequence generation without changing the model weights. However, existing methods typically construct steering vectors from global differences between property-positive and property-negative protein populations, overlooking how property-improving directions vary across different protein sequence backgrounds. To address this, we propose Paired-Unit local steering of embeddings (PULSE) , which matches positive- and negative-property proteins by maximizing their representation cosine similarity and constructs steering vectors by aggregating similarity-weighted, unit-normalized differences between matched pairs. Across three protein optimization objectives–solubility, immunogenicity, and toxicity– PULSE consistently outperforms global population-centroid steering in both final predicted property scores and optimization success rates. Further analysis reveals that conventional static steering-vector diagnostics cannot adequately explain optimization performance. To characterize steering reliability during iterative sequence editing, we introduce Local Directional Support (LDS) , which measures how well successive representation changes align with property-improving directions from similar protein backgrounds. We show that LDS captures differences in trajectory reliability and enables predictor-free candidate prioritization, enriching successful protein designs without requiring property predictions during candidate selection. Together, these findings demonstrate the importance of context-aware steering and trajectory-level evaluation for controllable protein sequence optimization.

title: Coarse-tuning to improve a protein foundation model for a domain of proteins: the example of outer membrane beta barrels
authors: Guy Yanai; Tomer Gan; Joanna S.G. Slusky; Margarita Osadchy; Rachel Kolodny
abstract: Foundation models for proteins have shown great potential in addressing a wide range of challenges in computational molecular biology. State-of-the-art models are trained on large and diverse corpora of protein sequences, enabled by self-supervised training. The models are then used in transfer learning and the embeddings they calculate are used in supervised downstream tasks. We propose a novel focusing mechanism for foundation models, which we call ‘coarse-tuning’. In coarse-tuning, we further update the model, using a defined yet unlabeled, dataset to enhance its performance in a specific domain. We demonstrate this approach using Outer Membrane Beta Barrels (OMBBs) — proteins that are found in the distinct biophysical environment of the outer membrane. Our results show that coarse-tuned models outperform the original foundation model when applied to various transfer learning tasks. Additionally, we study the embeddings generated by the coarse-tuned models and compare them to those from the original foundation model, including an investigation of the learned attention matrices via contact map predictions. Our work suggests that a medium-sized dataset (fewer than 100,000 protein sequences) is sufficient to effectively specialize a foundation model to a specific domain, enhancing its utility for domain-specific applications.

title: Learning the limits of protein structure models with NMR chemical shifts
authors: Cizhang Zhao; Gina El Nesr; Yilin Chen; Hannah K Wayment-Steele
abstract: Protein foundation models are intended to implicitly learn the chemical rules underlying protein function. However, systematically evaluating what biochemistry these models have learned remains difficult, as most downstream tasks lack experimental data fine-grained enough to expose their failure modes. NMR chemical shifts fill this gap: as direct per-atom reporters of local chemical environment, they offer a sensitive probe of structure-based representations. In this work, we present a systematically curated chemical shift dataset designed to minimize experimental confounders. We use it to benchmark diverse protein foundation models in their ability to predict backbone 15N chemical shifts, atoms that are known to be sensitive to many effects. The largest error across all models is in core residues with evidence of fast-timescale dynamics, which we investigate mechanistically using molecular dynamics simulations. Given the biological relevance of structured dynamic regions, we trained a new model based on the best of these embeddings, SLAE, to predict its own error. SLAE-ERR achieves a mean absolute error of 0.76 ppm for predicting error. Together, we hope that the datasets, evaluation tasks, and models presented here are sources of guidance for protein design model improvement.

title: Binary Patterning as a Probe of Protein Language Model Representations
authors: Dylan Klein; Michael Hecht; Vikas Nanda
abstract: Do protein language models (pLMs) encode the physical rules that govern protein folding? The four-helix bundle provides a classic test case because binary patterning, the ordered placement of polar and nonpolar residues along an amphipathic α-helix, is sufficient to generate folded proteins with high probability. Here, we ask whether ESM2 captures the sequence grammar underlying this design strategy. Libraries of synthetic sequences constrained only by binary patterning were predicted by ESMFold to form four-helix bundles. Predicted helicity, compactness, and topological diversity changed with sequence length in the same direction as experimentally characterized libraries, although the model did not distinguish successful from unsuccessful individual designs. Principal component analysis of ESM2 embeddings revealed representations of hydrophobic patterning, helix-loop boundaries, and heptad register. Extending the analysis to all 128 heptad binary patterns produced a jellyfish-shaped manifold in which hydrophobic composition formed the dominant axis, while paired components encoded pattern phase. Manifold geometry depended on amino-acid chemistry, repeat number, and linker sequence, and collapsed when amino acids were assigned to arbitrary categories. ESM2 therefore combines general repeat recognition with protein-specific physicochemical information. More broadly, synthetic sequence libraries provide experimentally grounded probes of protein language model representations and their relationship to protein biophysics.

title: The Confessions of a Protein Language Model: Steering, Activations, and What Predicted Confidence Cannot Certify
authors: Panini Shah; Raj Panchali; Pearl Mody; Mahek Sanghvi; Meera Narvekar; Ruhina Karani
abstract: Protein generate-and-screen pipelines use interventions and readouts to select candidates, but rarely test whether these track their intended targets. We audit published repetition steering, ESMFold confidence, and an activation readout. Steering preserves confidence at its operating point, but a fitted cliff follows at alpha_50 = 1.240x (sweep's own control: 64.0%). Direction matters at moderate matched-norm push, but not at saturation. Unsteered generator activations predict the confidence gate (ROC-AUC 0.786 +/- 0.004), supporting cost-aware, model-specific triage. We also replicate established length sensitivity, through which shortening can manufacture false nulls. Yet on composition- and length-matched design--scramble pairs, no balanced-accuracy interval excludes chance for experimental stability. Predicting the gate does not establish foldability. We should test what a readout measures before using it to select. Code and data: https://github.com/paninishah/plm-steering-audit

title: Rapid generation of antibody conformational ensembles using machine learning
authors: Rao PV; Sommer D; Davidson D; Alberstein RG; Ludwiczak J; Kleinhenz J; Vani B; Park E; Lee JH; Izadi S; Kiefer JR; Bonneau R; Mahajan SP; Watkins AM; Dreyer FA
abstract: We introduce Cadense, a generative framework for antibody ensemble prediction that produces diverse Fv structures from sequence, informed by conformational dynamics. While a valuable resource, static structure prediction provides only a single snapshot of dynamic proteins, whose motions influence their binding and other properties. This is particularly relevant for antibodies, an important class of molecules for drug discovery, where flexible complementarity determining region (CDR) loops are difficult to model with static approaches. Cadense addresses this gap by generating ensembles that match conformational and biophysical property distributions from molecular dynamics (MD), while reducing the computational burden from days of simulation to seconds of generation. We show Cadense ensembles can recover both apo and holo conformations of the same antibody and serve as effective input to physics-based docking, capturing the conformational flexibility important to properly model antibody–antigen interactions. Together, these results establish Cadense as a useful tool for antibody conformational ensemble generation with the promise to enable faster, dynamics-aware antibody design.

title: Leveraging state-of-the-art AI structure predictors to generate atomic resolution ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins
authors: Schnapka V; Portal N; Bonomi M
abstract:
Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are central to many biological processes, but their function depends on dynamic conformational ensembles rather than a single structure. Despite the impact of artificial intelligence on protein structure prediction, determining these ensembles at atomistic resolution remains challenging. Recently, we introduced bAIes, a framework that leverages the structural information encoded in AlphaFold2 distograms to generate conformational ensembles of IDPs at atomistic resolution. Here, we extend this framework to six state-of-the-art structure prediction tools (AlphaFold2, AlphaFold3, Boltz-1, Boltz-2, ESMFold, and ESMFold2) and systematically compare the structural information encoded in their predicted inter-residue distance distributions. Despite differences between predictors, we show that bAIes generates ensembles with comparable accuracy against experimental NMR and SAXS data, and competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art all-atom simulations and alternative IDP ensemble generation methods. These results demonstrate that bAIes is robust to the choice of structure predictor and that the distance distributions generated by different deep learning architectures contain valuable information about the conformational preferences of disordered proteins. More broadly, our work highlights the potential of combining AI-derived structural information with physics-based modeling to generate atomistic ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins and regions.
