title: REVEAL: RNA Ensemble Validation and Exploration with AI-guided Landscapes
authors: Bhakat S; Vats S
abstract: Capturing the sparsely populated but functionally important, excited states of RNA remains a central challenge for molecular simulation, because the underlying transitions are rare events that unbiased molecular dynamics cannot reach from a single starting structure. Here we introduce REVEAL (RNA Ensemble Validation and Exploration with AI-guided Landscapes), a workflow that couples generative secondary structure sampling, secondary structure conditioned tertiary structure prediction with trRosettaRNA2, unbiased molecular dynamics and Markov state modeling. Using only the sequence of the engineered HIV-1 TAR mutant, in which the excited state ES2 is the dominant conformation, we show that REVEAL captures the reversible ES2 to GS register shift from 6.8 µs of aggregate unbiased sampling across 34 seeds, recovering both basins, the intermediate states, and correctly identifies ES2 as the dominant state, consistent with the design of the construct. In contrast, molecular dynamics seeded from the ES2-dominant HIV-1 TAR mutant NMR ensemble remains trapped in ES2 despite substantially longer aggregate simulation time, and sequence-only ensemble predictors (AlphaFold3, Boltz-2, ESMFold2, OpenFold3 and Protenix-v2) place every structure near the ground state and invert the experimentally observed population ordering. The information content of the seed ensemble, rather than the total simulation time, determines whether the transition is sampled. We further introduce “ population-weighted consensus score ” (PWCS) that ranks conformers by how representative they are of the equilibrium ensemble directly from the simulation data, without experimental restraints and independent of the choice of collective variables. PWCS identifies the dominant state even when low-dimensional representations fail to separate the states. Built entirely from open-source tools, REVEAL provides a transparent and extensible route to RNA conformational ensembles beyond the single-structure paradigm.

title: Uncovering Features of ProteinMPNN with Sparse Autoencoders
authors: Mukkavilli N; Ivanov K; Anastasiu DC; Beck DAC; Akbari H; McCully M
abstract: Customization and modification of machine learning derived sequences can be achieved by understanding the mechanics behind state-of-the-art protein design models such as ProteinMPNN. Uninterpretability is hypothesized to be due largely to polysemanticity where neural networks store more features than they have dimensions. Here, we introduce sparse autoencoders (SAEs) into ProteinMPNN which expand its latent space and uncovers correlations between the activations in sparse dimensions and the presence of protein features such as secondary structure, residue volume, residue shape, disulfide bridges, and coordination to ligands. Additionally, we show that sparse activations can be manipulated to produce a variant of the short chain variable fragment Brolucizumab that is more thermostable than variants produced by traditional machine learning methods based on high temperature molecular dynamics simulations. Thus, SAEs provide both mechanistic understanding of protein design models and allow customizable manipulation of sequence prediction.

title: Inter-domain flexibility in F-Box proteins revealed by integrative modeling
authors: Shor B; Jiao F; Shi H; Mao H; Yu C; Braitbard M; Huang L; Zheng N; Schneidman-Duhovny D
abstract: F-box proteins, the substrate-recognition modules of the SCF (Skp1-Cul1-F-box) ubiquitin ligase complex, play a central role in targeted protein degradation by enabling the selective recruitment of diverse substrates. F-box proteins share a common architecture with a conserved anchor domain linked to the substrate-binding domain. Despite extensive structural characterization of F-box proteins, their potential conformational dynamics remain poorly understood. Here, we employ an integrative modeling approach combining cryo-EM structures, cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS), and deep learning-based conformational ensemble prediction to profile the accessible conformations of F-box proteins. Our analyses reveal a significant inter-domain flexibility in FBXL2 and FBXL17 that enables sampling of a broad range of conformations within assembled SCF and CSN-SCF complexes. By contrast, other F-box proteins, including FBXL1 and FBXO22, exhibit intrinsic flexibility but are restricted to a considerably narrower conformational landscape. Together, our work highlights inter-domain plasticity as a tunable architectural feature of F-box proteins, which may shape their functional versatility within SCF complexes.

title: Membrane Geometry Reveals Strengths and Limitations of AlphaFold-Predicted Transmembrane Protein Complexes
authors: Sziklai D; Wiener Z; Padanyi R; Hegedűs T
abstract: High-confidence protein complex predictions do not necessarily represent physically or biologically plausible assemblies. This limitation is particularly relevant for transmembrane (TM) proteins, whose interactions are constrained by the lipid bilayer. Here, we systematically evaluated membrane compatibility in the recently expanded AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, analysing 189,469 high-confidence AlphaFold-Multimer TM-TM complexes and additional TM-soluble assemblies. Most predictions exhibited plausible membrane geometry: among 125,657 evaluable complexes with TM proteins possessing more than two TM helices, 95.4% had joint hydrophobic thicknesses within the expected range of 15-35 angstroms. Nevertheless, some complexes displayed substantial inconsistencies in membrane positioning or protomer orientation despite favourable prediction confidence. Interactions between TM proteins, particularly those containing only one or two TM helices, were frequently dominated by extramembrane contacts. Among TM-soluble complexes, 77.4% showed no penetration of the soluble partner into the hydrophobic membrane core. We further investigated whether AlphaFold3 (AF3) could overcome limitations of AlphaFold-Multimer. Although AF3 recovered an experimentally supported SERCA-phospholamban interaction, it failed to reproduce the cholesterol-mediated norepinephrine transporter homodimer. A benchmark of 173 cholesterol-containing membrane protein targets further revealed limited accuracy in predicting cholesterol-binding poses, particularly for structures released after the AF3 training cutoff. Together, these findings demonstrate that membrane-specific geometric constraints provide a valuable complement to conventional confidence metrics and highlight the persistent challenges of predicting assemblies involving lipids.

title: Generative design of de novo AAV vectors with unique serological profiles
authors: Chiesa G; Lyu S; Nguyen MD; Benjamin J; Garton M
abstract: More than 5000 monogenic diseases are potentially curable by replacing a single defective gene with one that functions normally. Currently, the only clinically approved vector able to effectively deliver a therapeutic gene to a target tissue is Adeno-Associated Viruses (AAVs). However, despite decades of work, only a handful of gene replacement therapies have been approved, and many patients remain ineligible for even those. A major barrier to broad adoption of AAV therapies is pre-existing immunity to AAVs, mediated by neutralizing antibodies (nAbs). It is potentially possible to change exposed capsid surfaces in AAV capsids to avoid nAb recognition. However, traditional techniques such as rational design and directed evolution only allow modest changes. AAV function becomes compromised long before full nAb avoidance is achieved. Recent advances in protein design by generative modelling provide a new way to overcome this problem by learning AAV design constraints from natural sequences. We built a variational autoencoder that could learn these sequence constraints and generate functional AAV capsid proteins de novo . More than 255 designs were synthesized and tested in vitro in two design sets, with one set dedicated to exploring uncertain regions of the sequence space. Between the two campaigns, seven designs transduced human cells with >50% efficiency, of which four avoided nAb neutralization (NT50 < 1:50) in all human sera that were reactive to AAV. In one of these designs, sequence identity to the nearest natural AAV sequence was 18% divergent. Given the radical sequence diversity and its unique serological profile, this new capsid design would represent the first ever AAV serotype designed de novo .

title: Pallatom2: Navigating the De Novo Protein Universe with Atom-to-Atom Modeling
authors: Guan J; Ma R; Lin S; Wei Y; Jin J; Ye W; Liu D; Wang H; Wu W
abstract: Protein binder design requires precise coordination of molecular structure, binding geometry, and experimentally measurable performance. We introduce Pallatom2, an efficient, precise Atom-to-Atom generative model that jointly models protein sequence, backbone conformation, side-chain geometry, and target-interface contacts. A unified Atom14 representation and residue-guided sparse all-atom attention enable bidirectional information exchange between residue-level and atom-level representations, coordinating global structure with local atomic detail in a compact model of just 65.9 million parameters. Its conditioning system provides fine-grained control over binder-target engagement and global and local protein conformations, supporting diverse target-specific design requirements. In silico evaluation demonstrates broad generative capability across long-chain monomers, multi-domain proteins, and homomultimers, with monomer sampling extending to 1,600 residues. In binder design, Pallatom2 achieves state-of-the-art in silico screening performance across all nine targets with cross-method benchmark data under the reported protocols. These in silico results translate into substantial experimental success: biolayer interferometry identifies 112 active designs among 210 tested candidates (53.3%), with binders obtained for all ten experimentally evaluated targets. Six targets yield picomolar-scale apparent affinities, including K_D values of 3.96 pM for SC2RBD and 33.8 pM for PD-L1, while TNFα reaches 1.166 nM. Beyond de novo discovery, starting-interface-guided BCMA design preserves association kinetics despite substantial sequence divergence; partial diffusion improves TNFα affinity by up to 7.57-fold; and CDR-associated interface remodeling converts an inactive de novo nanobody into binders with apparent K_D values of 4.31 and 5.93 nM. Together, these results establish Pallatom2 as a versatile model for protein design, combining efficient atomic modeling, leading in silico screening performance, and experimentally demonstrated capabilities in high-affinity binder discovery, interface transfer, affinity maturation, and recovery of inactive designs.

title: Library of peptides: Analysis of a complex reactive mixture with the use of statistical physics and inference
authors: Laura Messio; Taleen Peker; Roba Moumné; Hélène Berthoumieux
abstract: Self-assembled mixtures enable the exploration of vast chemical diversity, yet characterizing the hundreds of coexisting species they contain remains a major challenge. Standard analytical techniques such as chromatography and spectroscopy produce overlapping signals that cannot be resolved by conventional deconvolution methods, which neglect the concentration correlations imposed by the reactive network. Here, we introduce a framework that bridges statistical physics and analytical chemistry to deconvolute complex self-assembled mixtures from partial spectral data. Inspired by Potts models of protein folding, we express the chemical potential of each compound as a function of a reduced set of parameters-intrinsic building-block energies and pairwise coupling terms between neighboring building blocks in the sequence. Coupling this model with the law of mass action yields equilibrium concentrations across the entire reactive network. The model parameters can be infered by fitting predicted spectroscopic signals to experimentally measured partial data. We demonstrate this approach using dynamic combinatorial libraries (DCLs) of peptides as a model system. Applied to a DCL of 81 peptides, our method resolves the full mixture composition from just 13 overlapping peaks, revealing that lateral couplings dominate the assembly energetics. Beyond DCLs, this strategy offers a general route for analyzing self-assembled systems from partial data and extends naturally to target-driven identification of high-affinity binders.

title: UV and deep-UV ultrafast harmonic generation enhanced by resonant gold nano-pillar metasurface
authors: Shroddha Mukhopadhyay; Yuxuan Chen; Hooman Barati Sedeh; Natalia M. Litchinister; Michael Scalora; Jose Trull; Maria Antonietta Vincenti; Crina Cojocaru
abstract: We report experimental observations and full-vector numerical simulations of second and third-harmonic generation from a two-dimensional periodic gold nano-pillar metasurface, for efficient ultrafast light conversion from near-infrared to the UV and deep-UV spectral ranges. The metasurface is designed to support an angle-tunable plasmonic resonance in the near-infrared spectral range, with its resonance wavelength shifting as a function of the pump angle of incidence. Under resonant conditions, strong electromagnetic-field confinement near the nano-pillar corners enhances the nonlinear light-matter interactions. Compared with a flat gold mirror, the nanostructured metal exhibits enhanced nonlinear frequency conversion, with conversion efficiencies of second and third-harmonic generation increased by two and three orders of magnitude, respectively. Full-wave theoretical modeling of linear and nonlinear light-matter interaction in nanoscale structures validates the experimental results. We demonstrate that periodically arranged square gold pillars can be engineered to achieve enhanced second and third-harmonic generation at wavelengths that can be tailored through the structural design, without requiring complex geometries or hybrid structures that pose fabrication challenges. The close agreement between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements further advances our understanding of surface-mediated nonlinear optical processes in metals and highlights the potential of metallic nanostructures as ultrafast light sources in the UV and deep-UV.

title: AI for Biologists: The Knowledge Boundaries of Foundation Models in the Age of Agentic Systems
authors: Tian Cai; Andrew Kleist; Jaimin Patel; Duccio Malinverni; Alexander K. Taylor; Malvika Sharan; Renato Umeton; M. Madan Babu
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how biological research is done. Biological foundation models trained on millions of nucleotides, protein, and single-cell measurements predict protein structures, mutation effects, and cellular responses to genetic perturbations. Agentic systems, AI assistants built on large language models, can run multistep analyses from plain-language requests and increasingly call foundation models as tools. Yet it is often unclear when these models' outputs can be trusted. We frame this as a model's knowledge boundary: the range of inputs, tasks, and conditions over which its outputs are reliable. This review explains how foundation models are built and proposes that five design elements (data, architecture, training scheme, evaluation scheme, and post-analysis) define this boundary. We examine evidence on where current models succeed or fail and present standardized descriptions of model limits so that researchers, and the agents acting for them, can use these tools reliably.

title: ControlHarbor: A Benchmark for Control Design by Coding Agents
authors: Jieqiang Wei; Fahad Ali; Jonny Reichwald; Silun Zhang
abstract: LLM agents, i.e., language models run by a harness, can now write, run and debug software autonomously. This raises the question of whether they can also carry out control system design. In this paper, we consider control system design as a task for LLM agents and grade the designed controller as control engineers do: the controller is given in a single Python file mapping measurements to actions, evaluated on held-out seeds against an ordered set of requirements, under specified physical perturbations and structural certificates, without using neural networks. We formulate the task as a chance-constrained feasibility problem and instantiate it in ControlHarbor, a benchmark of 44 tasks over 13 plants, which includes network consensus, vehicle platooning, the MuJoCo hopper, walker and humanoid. The tasks are packaged in the Harbor format, so that any agent harness can be run against them, and the same environments also serve learning algorithms other than LLMs, such as reinforcement learning (RL), under the same evaluation. With ControlHarbor, we observe that the controllers designed by three frontier coding agents, Claude Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Sonnet 5.5, reach the RL return on every parity task, but only in a minority of sessions. We also observe that the controllers certified for return alone usually fail under perturbations. When robustness is part of the specification, a structured design meets it at the RL return on the humanoid task, where domain-randomised RL does not; under large pushes, domain-randomised RL succeeds and no designed controller does. The benchmark, the controllers, and their grades are released.

title: MutAtlas: A PDB-Wide Energy-Guided Atlas of Protein Mutation Effects
authors: Ruihan Guo; Chaoran Cheng; Zhanghan Ni; Neil He; Bangji Yang; Ge Liu
abstract: Protein mutation effect prediction is fundamental to protein engineering and disease variant interpretation, yet experimentally measured mutation data remain accurate but extremely sparse. To provide scalable supplementary mutation signals, we construct a PDB-wide mutation augmentation dataset that exhaustively enumerates single-site substitutions on experimentally resolved protein structures and aligns mutation signals from physics-based energy models, protein language models, and inverse folding models. Large-scale analysis under a unified mutation preference representation reveals substantial differences in the consistency, concentration, and substitution patterns of mutation distributions across models, indicating that disagreement is pervasive and reflects conflicting inductive biases rather than random noise. Motivated by these observations, we propose an unsupervised multi-source mutation preference distillation framework that learns from relative mutation preferences while explicitly modeling cross-source disagreement. Without using any experimental mutation labels during training, our approach achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated zero-shot baselines and naive multi-source fusion strategies on ProteinGym. We release the dataset and evaluation pipeline to support reproducible studies of protein mutation effects.

title: Expanding the Decision Space of Pretrained Models through Structured Re-Decoding
authors: Tinglan Wang; Qun Su; Shihang Wang; Chi Wang; Lin Wang; Shaobo Chen; Haixu Liu; Hai Wei; Yin Ma; Yu Kang; Qi Gao; Xiaojun Yao; Tingjun Hou; Kai Wen
abstract: Native decoders limit how pretrained models combine local predictions under new structural constraints. We introduce Structured Re-Decoding (SRD), a training-free framework that constructs local candidates from model scores, samples, or external specifications, jointly optimizes their selection, and verifies reconstructed outputs. We show that candidate recombination expands feasible support and can improve attainable reward under a fixed KL divergence budget. Across molecular generation, protein design, RNA structure prediction, and antibody modeling, SRD enables improved structured inference, including verified molecules absent from the original sample pool. External chemical templates further extend SRD to noncanonical amino acids, peptide cyclization, and grammar-guided molecular construction. Preliminary experiments on a physical coherent Ising machine demonstrate the feasibility of hardware-based optimization, suggesting broader opportunities for quantum and quantum-inspired approaches to structured inference and combinatorial optimization across scientific domains.

title: ANTIOCH-VS: From Sequence to Hits with Modular, Open-Source Ensemble Virtual Screening
authors: Hale S. Hasdemir; Venkata Sai Sreyas Adury; Pratyush Tiwary
abstract: Structure-based virtual screening needs a receptor conformation that fits the ligand class, but for most targets no ligand-bound crystal is available -- and a single predicted model or an apo structure often misses the binding-competent state. We present ANTIOCH-VS, an open-source framework that runs an entire in silico screening campaign, from a protein sequence to a ranked shortlist of candidate binders, as one plug-and-play workflow. It first builds a conformational ensemble by reduced-MSA subsampling with ColabFold, then uses AlphaFold2-RAVE (AF2RAVE) -- short molecular-dynamics simulations with State Predictive Information Bottleneck analysis -- to pick out docking-ready, Boltzmann-weighted metastable states. It then detects the binding pocket, prepares receptors and ligands, docks the library across the ensemble with DOCK6 or AutoDock Vina, builds a consensus ranking, and triages the top hits by physics-based metadynamics (CTMD). We benchmark it on two very different targets, JAK2 kinase and ADRB2 GPCR, using their DUD-E benchmark sets of known binders and property-matched decoys. Starting from sequence alone -- no ligand-bound crystal, no manual intervention -- the AF2RAVE ensembles gave top-20 shortlists strongly enriched for true binders: a 20% hit rate for JAK2 and 60% for ADRB2 (random ~1-2%), on par with ligand-bound crystals and, for the kinase, above single AF2 models and an apo crystal. The full pipeline runs end to end on a workstation or HPC from a single command, or each module can be run on its own with user-supplied inputs. ANTIOCH-VS is freely available at https://github.com/tiwarylab/antioch-vs

title: How anion composition governs structural frameworks and Li-ion transport in oxychloride solid-state electrolytes
authors: Jiho Lee; Seungwoo Hwang; Seungwu Han; Jisu Jung; Youngho Kang; Sungwoo Kang
abstract: Mixed-anion lithium oxychlorides exhibit high Li conductivity, but the relationship between oxygen content, structural framework, and Li-ion transport remains unclear. Here, crystal structure prediction and molecular dynamics simulations with machine-learning interatomic potentials are used to examine $\mathrm{Li}_yM\mathrm{O}_x\mathrm{Cl}_{6-2x}$ ($M$ = Nb and Ta [Group 5] and $M$ = Ti, Zr, and Hf [Group 4]). Increasing oxygen content changes isolated chloride-rich polyhedra into one-dimensional chains and subsequently more highly connected two- and three-dimensional frameworks. In the Group 5 series, fast Li diffusion occurs over $x \approx 0.67$--1.5, where the Li sites form a three-dimensional percolating network. Potential of mean force maps and nudged elastic band calculations reveal that fast Li-ion transport requires a low-dimensional framework supporting long-range migration through undercoordinated Li sites with low barriers, together with similar energies across Li sites. Finally, we perform fine-grid compositional search, which identifies $\mathrm{LiNbO}_{0.67}\mathrm{Cl}_{4.67}$, $\mathrm{LiTaO}_{0.75}\mathrm{Cl}_{4.5}$, $\mathrm{LiNbO}_{1.5}\mathrm{Cl}_3$, and $\mathrm{LiTaO}_{1.5}\mathrm{Cl}_3$ as stable candidates with predicted room-temperature self-diffusivities of up to $\sim 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{cm}^2/\mathrm{s}$. These findings establish how oxygen content controls framework and Li-ion transport, guiding the design of lithium oxyhalide electrolytes.

title: Unidentified Sources in the 4FGL-DR4 Fermi-LAT Catalog as Potential Dark Matter Satellites
authors: Fernando Valenciano; Miguel A. Sánchez-Conde; Jorge Martin Camalich
abstract: The nature of dark matter (DM) remains unknown, standing as one of the most pressing questions in modern physics. We focus on indirect DM detection via gamma-ray emission from annihilating weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs). Within the $Λ$CDM cosmological framework, the hierarchical assembly of structure predicts a rich population of DM halos and subhalos. If WIMPs compose DM, annihilation inside these subhalos would generate gamma rays that could be detectable by instruments such as the Fermi-LAT. Since 2008, Fermi-LAT has cataloged several thousand of gamma-ray sources, with a third lacking clear astrophysical association. Some of these unassociated sources (unIDs) may actually be dark satellites, i.e., Galactic subhalos not massive enough to retain gas or stars and thus with no counterparts at other wavelengths. Starting from the 14-year Fermi-LAT catalog (4FGL-DR4), we conduct a systematic search for dark satellite candidates among its 2428 unIDs. We first design and apply a series of filters based on expected properties of dark satellites to reduce our sample. Through an exhaustive spectral Fermi-LAT data analysis, we find that none of the remaining unIDs shows a statistically significant preference for a DM interpretation. We place conservative constraints on the $\langleσv\rangle-m_χ$ DM parameter space, which are a factor of 2-3 above the thermal relic cross section value at the lowest WIMP masses in a conservative scenario, and rule out thermally-produced WIMPs below $\sim$50 GeV in the $b\bar{b}$ channel when assuming the sensitivity reach of the method. Our results emphasize the distinctive value of unID-based searches: they yield constraints that complement those derived from classical DM targets, such as dwarf spheroidal galaxies, and probe a unique, cosmologically motivated population of dark satellites otherwise inaccessible to observations.

title: Deep learning-guided discovery reveals the diversity and mutational potential of environmental beta-lactamases
authors: Liangjun Ge; Qiandi Gao; Haiming Xu; Zhiwei Qin; Heqian Zhang
abstract: Beta-lactamases are a major mechanism of bacterial resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics; however, their functional diversity and mutational potential in environmental microbial communities remain partially understood. This study aimed to characterize environmental beta-lactamase diversity and investigate how sequence variation influences antibiotic resistance. By integrating protein language model (PLMs) with ensemble learning, we identified more than 46,000 putative beta-lactamases across all four Ambler classes from environmental metagenomes, widely distributed across diverse habitats, with distinct habitat-associated class compositions. The candidates sharing approximately 30% sequence identity with known beta-lactamases conferred resistance to multiple beta-lactam antibiotics when expressed in Escherichia coli. Combining inverse folding model with PLMs further identified mutations that altered resistance profiles, including substitutions that increased resistance to carbapenems. Predicted high-fitness sites exhibited greater natural sequence variability overall, with higher variability in wastewater-derived than ocean-derived enzymes. These findings reveal undercharacterized beta-lactamase diversity and substantial mutational flexibility in environmental microbiomes, providing a basis for investigating their potential contribution to the diversification of antibiotic resistance.

title: HyInv Technical Report
authors: Haowei Lin; Cai Zhou; Xiangxin Zhou
abstract: Inverse folding designs amino-acid sequences for a given protein backbone, and screening needs many candidates that are both diverse and well folded. We present HyInv, a 1.96-million-parameter backbone-conditioned graph network with an encoder-decoder architecture, trained by Hyra 2.0, the research agent developed by our team: pretrained with random-order autoregressive sequence modeling, followed by structure-reward reinforcement learning. At inference, a grouped draft-and-rewrite sampler that uses separate draft and rewrite temperatures improves refolding TM-score at matched diversity. An optimized implementation with BF16 numerics designs 128 sequences for a 402-residue backbone in 50.6 ms on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU, about 52 times faster than the reference sampler, and an exact FP32 path that returns the reference sequences is 8.7 times faster. Across five benchmark datasets and seven dataset-predictor combinations, HyInv reaches a higher average scTM than all ten external baselines at comparable or higher sequence diversity, with large margins over ProteinMPNN and ProteinZero V2. The same default setting supports de novo backbones, pocket-constrained libraries, enzyme redesign with the catalytic site kept, and loop redesign. We have released our code and model at https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hyra-results/tree/main/AI4Science/hyinv.

title: OriDynamics: Towards a World Model for Biomolecular Dynamics
authors: Jiahao Yang; Dong Liu; Hongliang Li; Ji Chen; Yuehua Liu; Daoyun Ding; Duo An; Jun Li; Jiahua Rao; Ziqiao Zhang; Peicong Lin; Shuangjia Zheng
abstract: Biomolecular recognition and regulation depend on atomic interactions that change as molecular partners fluctuate and adopt alternative conformations. Modeling these processes requires ensembles that capture both conformational diversity and coordinated atomic fluctuations between interacting molecules. Here we present OriDynamics, a unified framework for all-atom ensemble generation across protein monomers and complexes with small molecules or protein partners. OriDynamics introduces a latent ensemble decomposition that couples broad conformational exploration in a compact structural latent space with local all-atom sampling around generated proposals. Ensemble-level supervision constrains mean positions, fluctuation amplitudes and joint coordinate covariance to capture coordinated atomic variability within and between molecular partners. Across benchmarks of proteins and their complexes, OriDynamics demonstrates superior overall performance in conformational coverage, atomic fluctuation fidelity and interaction geometry compared with leading baselines. Application studies further demonstrate recovery of alternative functional conformations and partner-dependent changes in conformational ensembles alongside sampling of configurations associated with ligand dissociation. These capabilities provide a foundation for a biomolecular world model that represents accessible molecular states and their dependence on interaction context.

title: Fine-Tuning a Graph-Transformer ADMET Model Improves Half-Life and Plasma Protein Binding Concordance
authors: Basel Mansour; Chetan Anand P; Binil Benny; Sifat Ahmed; Shayoni Dutta; Daniel Kei Takahashi
abstract: Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) models are usually judged on predefined benchmark splits. Those splits are useful, but they do not show whether a model reproduces the pharmacokinetic (PK) numbers that are actually reported for individual drugs. Here we compared ADMET-AI with a fine-tuned NV-KERMT-70M-v2 model (“KERMT”) on the same Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC)-aligned endpoint definitions. KERMT was fine-tuned in two stages: a protocol check on the ChEMBL multitask (ChEMBL-MT) data set, then TDC-aligned regression and classification fine-tuning on merged ChEMBL, Biogen, ExpansionRx/OpenADMET and TDC data. Two retrospective literature comparisons were run. The first used a curated 25-drug oncology panel: for half-life (n = 17) KERMT cut mean absolute error (MAE) from 46.81 to 16.83 h (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.0046, Holm-adjusted p = 0.0139, closer for 13 of 17 drugs); volume of distribution at steady state (VDss, n = 12) and hepatocyte clearance (n = 17) showed no statistically supported difference. The second, reported here for the first time, is an expanded three-way comparison of 53 oncology drugs × 3 endpoints (159 drug-endpoint rows) against curated literature and label values. On the 48 drugs with a usable half-life reference, KERMT more than halved the error (MAE 19.43 vs 43.38 h; median absolute error 12.01 vs 35.30 h; geometric mean fold error, GMFE, 2.72 vs 3.69; within 2-fold 41.0% vs 25.0%), was closer for 34 of 48 drugs (70.8%; 95% confidence interval, CI, 55.9-83.0%), and the paired Wilcoxon test was significant (p = 0.0002; Holm-adjusted p = 0.0004). The advantage persisted after each model's systematic bias was removed (p = 0.0004), so it is not a simple scale offset: ADMET-AI over-predicted half-life for 35 of 48 drugs (mean bias +29.20 h) whereas KERMT was mildly conservative (-13.79 h). For plasma protein binding ratio (PPBR, n = 21) KERMT had lower MAE (7.05 vs 9.44 percentage points) and the only statistically significant rank agreement with literature seen anywhere in this study (Spearman ρ = 0.540, p = 0.012, vs 0.400, p = 0.073), but the paired error difference was not significant (p = 0.157). One endpoint failed outright and we state it plainly: KERMT VDss predictions collapsed to near-baseline behaviour. They occupied a narrow band (46 of 53 drugs between 0 and 10 L/kg; standard deviation 3.64 vs 6.71 L/kg for ADMET-AI), no drug in the panel had an assay-matched VDss reference, and on the six drugs with an approximate reference the per-drug KERMT predictions (MAE 2.18 L/kg) were no better than replacing the entire model with one constant (MAE 2.14 L/kg) and worse than a no-information baseline (1.71 L/kg). KERMT VDss output should therefore not be used. A deliberately strict control bounds the positive findings as well: against a structure-blind constant predictor built by leave-one-out from the reference values, KERMT was statistically indistinguishable on both endpoints (half-life MAE 19.43 vs 16.07 h, p = 0.051; PPBR 7.05 vs 7.24 percentage points, p = 0.812), while ADMET-AI was significantly worse than that constant for half-life (p < 0.0001). We therefore make no claim of accurate numerical point prediction; the supported claims are that fine-tuning removes ADMET-AI's large systematic half-life error and that the PPBR rank correlation is compound-specific signal a constant cannot possess. Physically impossible values occurred in 16 of 159 KERMT rows and 21 of 159 ADMET-AI rows. Across 30 classification endpoints, mean inter-model Pearson correlation was 0.711 and mean binary agreement at 0.5 was 89%, which measures similarity, not accuracy. This version does not yet include official Therapeutics Data Commons benchmark-group evaluation of the fine-tuned models, replicate training seeds, or a training-set overlap audit; those gaps are declared explicitly rather than left implicit. The overall conclusion is endpoint-specific: fine-tuned KERMT is a materially better-calibrated half-life and plasma-protein-binding predictor than ADMET-AI on this panel, it is not yet a demonstrated ranking model for half-life, and its VDss head is unusable.
